ans.pattern: Heap / priority queue (repeatedly merge the two smallest)
ans.brute: Trying all merge orders is exponential; the greedy 'merge two smallest' is optimal (Huffman) and needs a min-heap.
ans.opt: Put all lengths in a min-heap. Repeatedly pop the two smallest, add their sum to the total, and push the sum back. Stop when one rope remains.

c13.title: Live Leaderboard
c13.story:
A game streams player scores one at a time as matches finish. After every score arrives, a spectator overlay must show the current Kth HIGHEST score among all scores seen so far -- not the top score, but the one sitting in Kth place from the top.

Early on, before at least K scores have arrived, there is no Kth-highest yet, and the overlay must show -1 for those moments. From the moment the Kth score arrives onward, every new score may or may not change the Kth-highest value, and the overlay updates accordingly.

Scores can repeat, and a repeated value occupies its own rank slot (three scores of 50 give a 1st, 2nd and 3rd place all equal to 50). Re-sorting everything after each arrival is far too slow for a long stream.

After each of the N arrivals, report the current Kth-highest score, using -1 until fewer than K scores have been seen.
inf: First line: two integers N K
Second line: N integers, the scores in arrival order
outf: A single line: N space-separated values, the running Kth-highest (or -1)
c13.exp: After 5: only one score, -1. After 1: scores {5,1}, 2nd highest = 1. After 8: {5,1,8}, 2nd highest = 5. After 3: {5,1,8,3}, 2nd highest = 5. Output: -1 1 5 5.

ans.pattern: Heap / priority queue (min-heap of the K largest)
ans.brute: Re-sorting the whole history each step is O(N^2 log N); a size-K min-heap keeps only what matters.
ans.opt: Maintain a min-heap capped at size K. Push each score; if the heap exceeds K, pop the smallest. Once it holds exactly K elements, its minimum (the root) is the Kth-highest; otherwise emit -1.

c14.title: Vault Maze
c14.story:
A courier drone must cross a vault floor laid out as an R by C grid. Each cell is either open ('.'), a solid wall ('#') the drone can never enter, the drone's start ('S'), or the exit ('E'). There is exactly one 'S' and one 'E', both on open floor.

The drone moves one cell at a time in the four orthogonal directions -- up, down, left, right -- and each such move takes one unit of time. It may never move diagonally and never pass through a wall or off the edge of the grid.

The operators want the FEWEST time units to travel from 'S' to 'E'. Because walls can form dead ends and long detours, and even wall off the exit entirely, the drone needs the true shortest route, not just any route. If no path of open cells connects 'S' to 'E', report -1.

Report the minimum number of moves from 'S' to 'E', or -1 if the exit is unreachable.
cons: the grid contains exactly one 'S' and one 'E'
inf: First line: two integers R C
Next R lines: the grid rows, each a string of length C
outf: A single integer: the fewest moves from S to E, or -1
c14.exp: The wall sits at the centre. A shortest route S(0,0) -> (0,1) -> (0,2) -> (1,2) -> (2,2)E takes 4 moves; no route is shorter. Answer 4.

ans.pattern: Graph: breadth-first search (unit-weight shortest path)
ans.brute: DFS does not give shortest paths; BFS explores by distance layers so the first time it reaches E is optimal.
ans.opt: BFS from S over open cells, tracking distance and visited. The distance stamped when E is first dequeued is the answer; if BFS drains without reaching E, output -1.

c15.title: Ferry Fares
c15.story:
An archipelago has N islands, numbered 1 to N, connected by M one-way ferry routes. Ferry route i runs FROM one island TO another (directed, because currents make the return trip a separate listed route) and charges a positive fare. A traveller starts on island S and wants to reach island D as cheaply as possible, changing ferries at intermediate islands as often as needed.

Because every fare is positive, a cheapest journey never revisits an island, but there can be many competing routes -- a longer chain of cheap hops may beat a single expensive direct ferry. Some islands may not be reachable from S at all.

There can be several ferry routes between the same ordered pair of islands with different fares, and you should of course use the cheaper when it helps.

Report the minimum total fare to travel from island S to island D, or -1 if D cannot be reached.
inf: First line: two integers N M
Second line: two integers S D
Next M lines: three integers u v w (a directed route u->v costing w)
outf: A single integer: the minimum fare from S to D, or -1
c15.exp: Routes from 1: 1->2->3->4 costs 2+1+2=5; 1->2->4 costs 2+7=9; 1->3->4 costs 5+2=7. The cheapest fare to island 4 is 5.

ans.pattern: Graph: Dijkstra (non-negative weights)
ans.brute: Enumerating routes is exponential; Bellman-Ford is O(N*M). Dijkstra with a heap is faster for non-negative fares.
ans.opt: Dijkstra from S: a min-heap of (cost, island), relaxing each outgoing route, skipping stale pops. Read off dist[D], or -1 if it stayed infinite.

c16.title: Assembly Dependencies
c16.story:
A factory builds a product from N assembly tasks, numbered 1 to N. There are M dependency rules; a rule 'a b' means task a must be fully finished before task b can begin. The dependencies are consistent -- there is no cycle -- so a valid overall order of tasks always exists.

Management wants to know the length of the CRITICAL CHAIN: the largest number of tasks that lie on a single dependency path, where each task in the path directly or indirectly depends on the previous one. This chain length is the minimum number of sequential stages the build must pass through even with unlimited parallel workers, because tasks on one chain cannot overlap.

A task with no dependencies is a chain of length one on its own, and independent tasks can be done in parallel, so they do not extend each other's chains.

Report the number of tasks on the longest dependency chain.
cons: 1 <= a, b <= N; the dependencies form a DAG
inf: First line: two integers N M
Next M lines: two integers a b (a must precede b)
outf: A single integer: the number of tasks on the longest chain
c16.exp: Chains through the DAG: 1->2->4 and 1->3->4 each pass through 3 tasks. No chain is longer, so the critical chain length is 3.

ans.pattern: Graph: topological sort + longest-path DP on the DAG
ans.brute: Trying all paths is exponential; processing nodes in topological order lets each chain length be computed once.
ans.opt: Kahn's topological order. Maintain chain[v] = longest chain ending at v, starting at 1. When relaxing edge u->v, chain[v]=max(chain[v], chain[u]+1). The answer is the maximum chain value.

c17.title: Balanced Books
c17.story:
An auditor examines a ledger of N daily net entries, each a signed integer (a credit is positive, a debit negative). A BALANCED SPAN is any contiguous run of days whose entries add up to exactly zero -- a stretch over which the credits and debits perfectly cancel.

The auditor wants a count of how many balanced spans exist anywhere in the ledger. Two spans that cover different day ranges are counted separately even if they happen to hold the same numbers, and a span must be a contiguous range of days -- you cannot skip a day in the middle.

Because entries can be negative, the running total is not monotone, so a grow-and-shrink window does not apply here: extending a span can lower its sum as easily as raise it. The ledger can be long, so scanning every possible span is too slow.

Report the number of contiguous balanced spans (those summing to exactly zero).
inf: First line: integer N
Second line: N integers, the daily entries
outf: A single integer: the number of zero-sum contiguous spans
c17.exp: Zero-sum spans: [1,-1] (days 1-2), [3,-3] (days 3-4), and [1,-1,3,-3] (days 1-4). That is 3 balanced spans.

ans.pattern: Prefix sum + hashmap of prefix frequencies
ans.brute: Summing every span is O(N^2). Equal prefix sums mark a zero-sum span between them.
ans.opt: Track a running prefix sum and a map of how often each prefix value has occurred (seed value 0 with count 1). For each new prefix, add the count of that same prefix already seen (each is a zero-sum span ending here), then record it.

c18.title: Ticker Spans
c18.story:
A trading terminal shows the daily closing price of a stock for N consecutive days. For each day the analyst wants its SPAN: the number of consecutive days ending on that day (and including it) over which the price was less than or equal to that day's price. In other words, starting from today and walking backward, how many days in a row have a price no greater than today's, until you hit a day with a strictly higher price or run off the start of the series.

The span of the very first day is always 1 (only itself). A day whose price is a fresh high over everything before it has a span equal to its 1-based position, since every earlier day was lower.

The series can be long, so comparing each day against all previous days would be quadratic; a structure that discards days which can never again dominate is expected.

Report the span for every day, in order, on a single line.
inf: First line: integer N
Second line: N integers, the daily prices
outf: A single line: N space-separated spans, one per day in order

ans.pattern: Monotonic stack (of indices with strictly decreasing price)
ans.brute: Scanning back from each day is O(N^2); a decreasing stack gives each span in amortised O(1).
ans.opt: Keep a stack of day indices whose prices strictly decrease. For each day, pop all indices whose price is <= today's; the span is the gap to the index now on top (or the day's position if the stack empties). Push the current index.

d1.title: Redundant Cabling
d1.story:
An electrician is wiring N junction boxes, numbered 1 to N, and lays down M cables one at a time, each cable directly joining two boxes. Once two boxes are joined -- directly or through a chain of other boxes -- current can flow between them, and this connectivity is transitive.

The budget office wants to flag WASTE. A cable is called redundant if, at the moment it is installed, the two boxes it joins are ALREADY connected through cables laid earlier -- installing it adds no new connectivity, it just loops back into an existing network. A cable that joins two previously separate networks (or a lone box to a network) is useful, not redundant.

Cables are processed strictly in installation order, and a redundant cable, though wasteful, is still installed and still present for later checks (it never changes who is connected to whom). Self-cables from a box to itself, if any appear, are redundant by definition.

Report how many of the M cables were redundant.
inf: First line: two integers N M
Next M lines: two integers a b, a cable
outf: A single integer: the number of redundant cables
d1.exp: (1,2) joins two boxes -> useful. (2,3) -> useful. (1,3): boxes 1 and 3 are already connected via 2 -> REDUNDANT. (3,4) -> useful. One redundant cable.

ans.pattern: Union-Find (DSU): a cable is redundant iff both endpoints already share a root
ans.brute: Re-checking connectivity by BFS per cable is O(M*(N+M)); DSU find is near-constant.
ans.opt: For each cable, find both roots. If they are equal, it is redundant; otherwise union them. Count the equal-root cases.

d2.title: Archipelago Count
d2.story:
A shallow sea is modelled as an R by C grid, entirely water at first. Engineers drop K loads of rock, each at a given cell, turning that cell into land; a load dropped on a cell that is already land is wasted and changes nothing. You may assume the drop coordinates are valid grid cells.

An ISLAND is a maximal group of land cells connected orthogonally -- up, down, left, right; cells that touch only at a corner are NOT connected and belong to different islands. As rock accumulates, a new land cell may start a fresh island, extend an existing one, or bridge two or more previously separate islands into a single larger island.

The survey team only wants the FINAL tally after all K loads have been dropped: how many distinct islands the sea ends up with.

Report the number of islands after all drops.
inf: First line: three integers R C K
Next K lines: two integers r c, a rock drop
outf: A single integer: the number of islands at the end
d2.exp: Cells (0,0) and (0,1) are orthogonally adjacent and form one island; (2,2) stands alone as a second island. Total 2 islands.

ans.pattern: Union-Find (DSU) over land cells (or a final flood fill)
ans.brute: Since only the final state matters, either union each new cell with its land neighbours, or flood-fill the final grid once.
ans.opt: Maintain a running island count: each new land cell adds one, then union it with each orthogonal land neighbour, decrementing the count on every successful merge. Duplicates are skipped.

d3.title: Warehouse Zoning
d3.story:
A single loading aisle holds N crates in a fixed line, crate i weighing a known amount; the crates cannot be reordered because they are stacked. The warehouse will assign K forklift crews, and each crew takes a CONTIGUOUS block of crates from the line -- crew 1 an opening run, crew 2 the next run, and so on -- so the K blocks partition the line in order with none skipping around.

Every crew works in parallel and a crew's finishing time is proportional to the total weight of its block, so the whole aisle is cleared only when the HEAVIEST-loaded crew finishes. The manager therefore wants to cut the line into K contiguous blocks so that the largest block-weight is as small as possible.

A single crate cannot be split between two crews, so the largest block can never be lighter than the heaviest single crate, no matter how many crews there are.

Report the minimum achievable value of the heaviest block-weight.
inf: First line: two integers N K
Second line: N integers, the crate weights in order
outf: A single integer: the minimised heaviest block-weight
d3.exp: Splitting as [7,2,5] and [10,8] gives block weights 14 and 18, largest 18. Every other 2-way contiguous split has a larger maximum (e.g. [7,2,5,10],[8] -> 24). So the answer is 18.

ans.pattern: Binary search on the answer (greedy block-count feasibility)
ans.brute: Interval DP over (crates, crews) is O(N^2*K); binary search on the cap is far faster.
ans.opt: Binary-search the cap X in [max weight, total weight]. Greedily count blocks by starting a new block whenever adding a crate would exceed X; feasible iff blocks <= K. Smallest feasible X is the answer.

d4.title: Conveyor Capacity
d4.story:
A shipping belt must send N parcels, in the exact order they sit on the belt, out over at most D days. Parcel i has a known weight. Each day the belt is loaded with a leading run of not-yet-shipped parcels whose total weight does not exceed the belt's daily capacity, then it runs and the day ends; parcels are never reordered and a parcel is never split across two days.

A larger daily capacity ships more parcels per day and so needs fewer days; a smaller capacity needs more days. The logistics team wants the SMALLEST daily capacity that still clears all N parcels within the D days available, to rent the least powerful belt that does the job.

Because the heaviest single parcel must fit on some day by itself, the capacity can never be less than the maximum parcel weight, regardless of D. The number of days needed falls monotonically as capacity rises.

Report the minimum daily belt capacity that ships everything within D days.
inf: First line: two integers N D
Second line: N integers, the parcel weights in belt order
outf: A single integer: the minimum daily capacity
d4.exp: With capacity 15 the parcels split into 5 days: [1,2,3,4,5]=15, [6,7]=13, [8]=8... in fact a valid 5-day packing exists at 15 and no smaller capacity fits everything in 5 days. Minimum capacity is 15.

ans.pattern: Binary search on the answer (greedy day-count feasibility)
ans.brute: Trying every capacity is O(sum*N); binary search makes the capacity dimension logarithmic.
ans.opt: Binary-search capacity in [max weight, total weight]. days(cap) greedily fills each day with a leading run under cap; feasible iff days <= D. Smallest feasible capacity wins.

d5.title: Fuel Loop
d5.story:
A racing circuit has N fuel depots arranged in a circle and numbered 0 to N-1 clockwise. Depot i holds gas[i] litres you may collect on arrival, and it costs cost[i] litres of fuel to drive from depot i clockwise to the next depot (from depot N-1 back to depot 0). A car with an unlimited tank but starting empty must complete one full clockwise lap, returning to where it began.

The car may choose ANY depot as its starting point. Beginning there with an empty tank, it collects that depot's gas, drives to the next (paying its cost), collects again, and so on all the way around. The tank must never go negative at any leg of the journey.

It is guaranteed that if a valid starting depot exists it is UNIQUE. If the total gas across all depots is less than the total driving cost, no start can complete the lap.

Report the 0-indexed starting depot from which a full lap is possible, or -1 if none exists.
inf: First line: integer N
Second line: N integers gas[i]
Third line: N integers cost[i]
outf: A single integer: the starting depot index, or -1
d5.exp: Total gas 15 equals total cost 15, so a lap is possible. Walking the running balance, the tank first stays non-negative for the whole loop when starting at depot 3. Answer 3.

ans.pattern: Greedy (single pass tracking a resettable running tank)
ans.brute: Trying each start and simulating a full lap is O(N^2); one linear pass suffices.
ans.opt: If total gas < total cost, return -1. Otherwise sweep once accumulating gas[i]-cost[i]; whenever the running tank drops below 0, the start cannot be at or before i, so reset the tank to 0 and set start=i+1. The final start is the unique answer.

d6.title: Stepping Stones
d6.story:
A frog sits on the first of N stepping stones laid in a straight line, numbered 0 to N-1. Stone i is engraved with a number a[i]: from stone i the frog may leap forward to any stone from i+1 up to i+a[i] (a leap of at least 1 and at most a[i] stones). The frog wants to reach the LAST stone.

Every leap, long or short, counts as one jump. The frog wants to reach stone N-1 in the FEWEST jumps. A greedy that always leaps as far as possible is not quite right; instead you track, within your current jump's reach, the farthest stone any next leap could take you to, and you spend a jump only when you must.

You may assume the last stone is always reachable. If the frog already starts on the last stone (N is 1), zero jumps are needed.

Report the minimum number of jumps to reach the last stone.
cons: the last stone is guaranteed reachable
inf: First line: integer N
Second line: N integers, the leap ranges a[i]
outf: A single integer: the minimum number of jumps
d6.exp: From stone 0 (range 2) the frog can reach stones 1 or 2; jumping to stone 1 (range 3) then reaches stone 4 in one more leap. That is 2 jumps, and no single-detour route is shorter.

ans.pattern: Greedy (BFS-by-layers over reachable ranges)
ans.brute: A DP over every (position) is O(N^2) in the worst case; the layered greedy is linear.
ans.opt: Sweep i from 0. Track 'far' = farthest index reachable using the current number of jumps. When i reaches the end of the current jump's range, spend one jump and extend the range to 'far'. Count the jumps.

d7.title: Spell Correction
d7.story:
A spell-checker must measure how far a typed word is from a dictionary word. You are given two strings A and B. In one operation you may INSERT a single character anywhere, DELETE a single character, or REPLACE one character with another. The distance between A and B is the minimum number of such operations that turns A exactly into B.

The checker uses this distance to rank suggestions -- a smaller distance means a closer match. Characters that already line up cost nothing; the operations are only spent where the two words disagree, and the cheapest alignment is not always obvious because an insertion in one place can save several replacements elsewhere.

Both strings consist of lowercase letters and may differ in length. Turning a word into itself costs 0, and turning any word into the empty string costs its length.

Report the minimum number of edit operations to transform A into B.
cons: A and B are lowercase letters
inf: First line: string A (may be empty)
Second line: string B (may be empty)
outf: A single integer: the edit distance
d7.exp: One optimal script: replace 'h'->'r' (horse->rorse), delete 'r' (rorse->rose... ), and delete 'e' -- three operations turn 'horse' into 'ros'. The edit distance is 3.

ans.pattern: Dynamic programming (Levenshtein table)
ans.brute: Trying all edit scripts is exponential; the 2-D DP over prefixes is polynomial.
ans.opt: dp[i][j] = distance between A's first i and B's first j characters. If the current characters match, dp[i][j]=dp[i-1][j-1]; else 1 + min(delete dp[i-1][j], insert dp[i][j-1], replace dp[i-1][j-1]).

d8.title: Best Trading Streak
d8.story:
An analyst has the daily PROFIT-OR-LOSS of a trading strategy for N consecutive days, each value positive (a gain) or negative (a loss). They want the best CONTIGUOUS streak: a run of consecutive days whose profits sum to the largest possible total.

The streak must be a contiguous block of days -- you cannot cherry-pick good days and skip the bad ones in the middle -- and it must contain at least one day. If every day is a loss, the best streak is simply the single least-bad day (its value, still negative), since a streak cannot be empty.

Extending a streak into a run of losses can drag its total down, so the trick is to know when to 'cut' and start a fresh streak. The series can be long, so an all-pairs scan of every possible streak is too slow.

Report the maximum sum achievable by any contiguous streak of days.
inf: First line: integer N
Second line: N integers, the daily profit/loss
outf: A single integer: the maximum contiguous streak sum
d8.exp: The contiguous streak [4,-1,2,1] sums to 6, the largest of any run. Answer 6.

ans.pattern: Dynamic programming (Kadane's running best)
ans.brute: Summing every subarray is O(N^2); Kadane keeps a single running best in one pass.
ans.opt: Track cur = best streak ending at the current day = max(value, cur+value), and best = max(best, cur). The overall best is the answer; starting both at the first value handles all-negative inputs.

d9.title: Exact Change
d9.story:
A cashier must hand back exactly A units of change using coins from a fixed set of denominations, each available in unlimited supply. Unlike counting the number of ways, here the cashier wants to use as FEW coins as possible -- fewer coins is faster to count out and lighter in the till.

The cashier may reuse any denomination as often as needed, and the order coins are handed over does not matter. A locally 'grab the biggest coin' rule can be wrong: with coins of 1, 3 and 4 making 6, greedily taking a 4 then two 1s uses three coins, while two 3s use only two.

If the amount A cannot be formed by any combination of the given denominations, report -1.

Report the minimum number of coins that sum to exactly A, or -1 if it is impossible.
inf: First line: the count of denominations and the amount A
Second line: the denominations
outf: A single integer: the minimum number of coins, or -1
d9.exp: Two coins of 3 make 6 using 2 coins; every other combination uses at least as many (4+1+1 uses 3). So the minimum is 2.

ans.pattern: Dynamic programming (unbounded coin change, minimise count)
ans.brute: Greedy fails for arbitrary denominations; the amount DP is exact.
ans.opt: dp[0]=0, dp[a]=1+min(dp[a-coin]) over coins that fit. Amounts left at infinity are unreachable; dp[A] is the answer or -1.

d10.title: Peak Attention Block
d10.story:
A streaming service logs the number of viewers who joined during each of N consecutive one-minute slots. A sponsor will buy a single advertising block that spans EXACTLY K consecutive minutes, and they want the block placed where it captures the most joined viewers in total.

So across all contiguous windows of K minutes, you must find the one whose viewer counts sum to the largest total. The window must be exactly K minutes wide and contiguous -- the sponsor cannot stitch together non-adjacent minutes.

Recomputing each window's sum from scratch is wasteful because consecutive windows overlap in K-1 minutes; sliding the window and adjusting by the one entering and one leaving minute is far faster.

Report the maximum total viewers over any window of K consecutive minutes.
inf: First line: two integers N K
Second line: N integers, the per-minute viewer counts
outf: A single integer: the maximum K-minute window sum
d10.exp: The window sums of size 3 are 8, 7, 9, 6. The window [5,1,3] gives 9, the maximum.

ans.pattern: Sliding window (fixed size, add one, drop one)
ans.brute: Summing each of the O(N) windows in O(K) is O(N*K); the fixed-window slide is linear.
ans.opt: Compute the first K-sum, then slide: for each new right index add a[i] and subtract a[i-K]. Track the maximum running window sum.

d11.title: Signal Uptime
d11.story:
A monitoring probe records N consecutive status ticks, each a 1 (the service was up that tick) or a 0 (it was down). The reliability team is allowed to RETROACTIVELY excuse at most K of the down ticks -- treating up to K zeros as if they had been ones -- to compute a best-case longest uptime streak for the report.

Concretely, find the length of the longest CONTIGUOUS run of ticks that contains at most K zeros, since those zeros can all be excused into ones, making the whole run count as uptime. The run must be contiguous; you cannot splice separate up-periods together.

K may be 0 (no excuses, so it is just the longest existing run of ones) or large enough to cover every zero (making the answer the whole length). Choosing WHICH zeros to excuse is exactly choosing where the window sits.

Report the length of the longest contiguous run containing at most K zeros.
inf: First line: two integers N K
Second line: N integers (0 or 1), the ticks
outf: A single integer: the longest run with at most K zeros
d11.exp: The window covering the first seven ticks [1,1,0,0,1,1,1] holds exactly two zeros, which K=2 can excuse, giving length 7. No window with <=2 zeros is longer.

ans.pattern: Sliding window (shrink when zero-count exceeds K)
ans.brute: Trying every window is O(N^2); a window that only shrinks when it has too many zeros is linear.
ans.opt: Expand the right end, counting zeros inside the window. Whenever zeros exceed K, advance the left end (decrementing the count as it passes a zero). Track the largest window width seen.

d12.title: Lecture Halls
d12.story:
A campus scheduler receives N lecture bookings for one day; booking i runs from start time s_i to end time e_i, occupying the half-open interval [s_i, e_i) -- a hall freed at time e_i can immediately host a lecture that starts at e_i, but two lectures whose times strictly overlap need separate halls.

The scheduler wants the MINIMUM number of halls needed so that every booking gets a room and no two overlapping bookings share one. This equals the greatest number of lectures that are ever in progress at the same instant.

Bookings arrive unsorted and may overlap in complicated ways -- nested, staggered, or back-to-back. A booking that starts exactly when another ends can reuse that hall.

Report the minimum number of halls required.
inf: First line: integer N
Next N lines: two integers s e, a booking
outf: A single integer: the minimum number of halls
d12.exp: Sorted by start: (0,30),(5,10),(15,20). (0,30) opens a hall. (5,10) overlaps it -> a 2nd hall (peak 2). (10) frees the 2nd; (15,20) reuses it. Peak simultaneous lectures is 2, so 2 halls.

ans.pattern: Heap / priority queue (min-heap of end times) or sweep-line
ans.brute: Comparing all pairs for overlap is O(N^2); a heap of active end times tracks concurrency directly.
ans.opt: Sort bookings by start. Keep a min-heap of end times of ongoing lectures. For each booking, pop all ended lectures (end <= its start), push its end, and record the heap size. The maximum size is the number of halls.

d13.title: Prize Cutoff
d13.story:
A contest ends with N players each holding a final score. The organisers award prizes to the top K scorers, and to print the cutoff notice they need the Kth HIGHEST score -- the score of the player in exactly Kth place from the top, which is the lowest score that still wins a prize.

Scores may repeat, and tied scores each occupy their own rank slot: if three players score 90, they fill the 1st, 2nd and 3rd prize positions, all worth 90. The organisers do not need the full ranking, only the single value sitting at position K.

K is guaranteed to be between 1 and N, so the Kth highest always exists.

Report the Kth highest score.
inf: First line: two integers N K
Second line: N integers, the scores
outf: A single integer: the Kth highest score
d13.exp: Sorted high to low: 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1. The 2nd highest is 5.

ans.pattern: Heap / priority queue (size-K min-heap) or quickselect
ans.brute: Fully sorting is O(N log N); a size-K min-heap or quickselect can do it in O(N log K) / average O(N).
ans.opt: Keep a min-heap of the K largest scores seen: push each score and pop the smallest whenever the heap exceeds K. The heap's root at the end is the Kth highest. (Sorting also works within limits.)

d14.title: Nearest Exit Drill
d14.story:
A building floor is an R by C grid. Each cell is an exit 'G', an open space '.', or a solid pillar '#'. During a drill, every person on an open space must walk to the NEAREST exit, moving one cell at a time up, down, left or right, never through a pillar or off the floor.

The safety officer wants the WORST case: over all open spaces, the largest 'distance to the nearest exit' (measured in steps). This single number bounds how long the slowest person needs to reach safety. There may be several exits, and each open space is served by whichever exit is closest to it.

If even one open space is completely walled off from every exit, the drill fails and the answer is -1. Exit and pillar cells themselves are not open spaces and do not count toward the worst case.

Report the maximum over open spaces of the distance to the nearest exit, or -1 if some open space cannot reach any exit.
cons: cells are 'G', '.', or '#'; at least one '.' exists
inf: First line: two integers R C
Next R lines: the grid rows
outf: A single integer: the worst nearest-exit distance, or -1
d14.exp: BFS from the single exit at (0,0) gives distances; the farthest open cell is (2,1) at distance 3 (the pillar at (2,2) is not an open space). Answer 3.

ans.pattern: Graph: multi-source BFS from all exits at once
ans.brute: Running a BFS from each open cell is O((RC)^2); one BFS seeded with all exits labels every cell with its nearest-exit distance.
ans.opt: Seed a queue with every exit at distance 0 and BFS outward, stamping the first (hence smallest) distance on each reachable cell. The answer is the max stamp over open cells, or -1 if any open cell stays unreached.

d15.title: Broadcast Delay
d15.story:
A control centre must push a firmware update out across N devices, numbered 1 to N, over M one-way network links. Link i carries a signal FROM one device TO another with a known transfer delay (directed, since the reverse link may not exist or may be slower). The update starts at a single source device S and propagates: as soon as a device receives it, it immediately forwards it along all its outgoing links.

A device receives the update at the EARLIEST time it can arrive by any path from S. The rollout is complete only when the LAST device has received it, so the completion time is the maximum over all devices of their earliest-arrival time.

Some devices may be unreachable from S entirely (no directed path), in which case the rollout can never complete.

Report the time at which every device has received the update, or -1 if some device is unreachable from S.
inf: First line: two integers N M
Second line: the source device S
Next M lines: three integers u v w (directed link u->v with delay w)
outf: A single integer: the completion time, or -1
d15.exp: Earliest arrivals from device 1: device2 at 1, device3 at min(4, 1+1)=2, device4 at 2+1=3. The last device receives it at time 3.

ans.pattern: Graph: Dijkstra, then take the maximum finalised distance
ans.brute: Enumerating paths is exponential; Dijkstra finds every earliest arrival in near-linear-log time.
ans.opt: Dijkstra from S over the directed weighted graph. The completion time is the maximum of all dist values; if any device is still infinite (unreached), output -1.

d16.title: Curriculum Check
d16.story:
A degree programme offers N courses labelled 0 to N-1. There are M prerequisite rules; a rule 'a b' means course a must be completed before course b can be taken. A student wants to know whether it is possible to complete ALL N courses in some order that respects every prerequisite.

If the prerequisite rules ever form a cycle -- course a needs b, b needs c, and c needs a, directly or through a longer loop -- then no valid order exists and the curriculum is impossible to finish. If there is no such cycle, some complete order always exists.

Rules may be repeated and a course may have many prerequisites or none. You do not need to output an order, only whether a valid one exists.

Print YES if all courses can be completed, otherwise NO.
inf: First line: two integers N M
Next M lines: two integers a b (a before b)
outf: YES if all courses can be completed, otherwise NO
d16.exp: Course 0 has no prerequisites; then 1 (needs 0), then 2 (needs 0 and 1). The order 0,1,2 works, so the answer is YES (there is no cycle).

ans.pattern: Graph: topological sort (Kahn) -- cycle detection
ans.brute: Trying orderings is exponential; Kahn's algorithm detects a cycle in linear time.
ans.opt: Compute in-degrees; repeatedly remove zero-in-degree nodes, decrementing neighbours. If every node is removed, no cycle exists (YES); if some remain stuck, a cycle blocks completion (NO).

d17.title: Target Windows
d17.story:
A fitness tracker logs the calories burned in each of N consecutive intervals, each value a signed integer (some intervals net negative after a correction). A coach wants to count how many CONTIGUOUS stretches of intervals burned exactly K calories in total -- a stretch being any run of consecutive intervals.

Two stretches covering different interval ranges count separately, even if they hold identical values, and a stretch must be contiguous with no interval skipped. Because values can be negative, the running total is not monotone, so a simple expanding-and-shrinking window does not work -- adding an interval can lower the running sum.

The log can be long, so checking every possible stretch directly is too slow.

Report the number of contiguous stretches whose values sum to exactly K.
inf: First line: two integers N K
Second line: N integers, the per-interval values
outf: A single integer: the number of stretches summing to exactly K
d17.exp: Prefix sums let us count stretches summing to 2: [1,1] over intervals 1-2 and [1,1] over intervals 2-3. That is 2 stretches.

ans.pattern: Prefix sum + hashmap of prefix frequencies
ans.brute: Summing every stretch is O(N^2); a prefix-frequency map makes it linear even with negatives.
ans.opt: Keep a running prefix sum and a map counting how often each prefix value has appeared (seed 0 -> 1). For each new prefix p, add the number of times (p - K) has been seen (each marks a stretch summing to K ending here), then record p.

d18.title: Next Taller Building
d18.story:
A city street has N buildings in a row, each with a given height. Standing on the roof of a building and looking to the RIGHT along the street, a resident wants to know the height of the FIRST building taller than their own -- the next building, scanning rightward, whose height is strictly greater. If no building to the right is taller, the view is open and the answer for that building is -1.

You must produce this 'next taller to the right' value for every building, in order. Equal-height buildings do not count as taller; only a strictly greater height blocks the view.

The street can be long, so comparing each building against all buildings to its right would be quadratic; a structure that keeps buildings still waiting for a taller neighbour is expected.

Report, for each building in order, the height of the next strictly taller building to its right, or -1 if there is none.
inf: First line: integer N
Second line: N integers, the building heights in order
outf: A single line: N space-separated values, the next taller height or -1
d18.exp: Building 0 (2): next taller is 4. Building 1 (1): next taller is 2. Building 2 (2): next taller is 4. Building 3 (4): none -> -1. Building 4 (3): none -> -1. Output: 4 2 4 -1 -1.

ans.pattern: Monotonic stack (decreasing heights awaiting a taller neighbour)
ans.brute: Scanning right from each building is O(N^2); a decreasing stack resolves each in amortised O(1).
ans.opt: Keep a stack of indices whose heights are non-increasing. For each new building, pop every stacked index shorter than it, setting their answer to the current height, then push the current index. Indices left on the stack get -1.

e1.title: Nested Crates
e1.story:
A shipping manifest encodes how crates are packed inside one another as a single string of bracket characters drawn from three crate families: round '(' ')', square '[' ']', and curly '{' '}'. An opening bracket means a crate of that family is opened and something is packed inside it; the matching closing bracket of the SAME family seals it. Crates must nest properly: the crate sealed by a closing bracket must be the most recently opened, still-open crate, and it must be of the same family.

A manifest is VALID only if every crate that is opened is later sealed by a matching closer, in correct nested order, with nothing left open at the end and no closer appearing with no matching open crate before it.

For a valid manifest, its NESTING DEPTH is the greatest number of crates open at the same moment while reading left to right. For an invalid manifest, there is no meaningful depth.

Report the maximum nesting depth if the manifest is valid, or -1 if it is invalid.
cons: S consists only of the characters ()[]{}
inf: A single line: the manifest string S
outf: A single integer: the maximum nesting depth, or -1 if invalid
e1.exp: Reading '[' opens depth 1, '(' opens depth 2 (the peak), ')' seals back to 1, ']' seals to 0, then '{' opens depth 1 and '}' seals to 0. Everything matches and nothing is left open, so it is valid with maximum depth 2.

ans.pattern: Simulation with a stack (validity + running depth)
ans.brute: A stack is the natural model; there is no shortcut past reading the whole string.
ans.opt: Push on each opener (tracking current and max depth); on a closer, fail if the stack is empty or its top is a different family, else pop. At the end, valid iff the stack is empty; report the max depth, else -1.

e2.title: Reveal-and-Rotate Deck
e2.story:
A magician holds a deck of N cards numbered 1 to N, stacked so that card 1 is on top and card N is on the bottom. The trick reveals the cards in a fixed mechanical way and you must predict the order in which they appear.

The magician repeats the following until the deck is empty: take the top card and place it face-up on the table (this is the next card revealed); then, if any cards remain, take the new top card and move it, unseen, to the BOTTOM of the deck. So the deck loses two cards' worth of attention each round -- one revealed, one buried -- until it runs out (the final round only reveals, with no card left to bury).

Crucially, the numbers on the cards are just 1..N in starting order; the reveal ORDER is what the trick scrambles.

Report the sequence of card numbers in the order they are revealed, space-separated.
inf: A single line: the integer N
outf: A single line: the revealed card numbers in order, space-separated
e2.exp: Deck top->bottom [1,2,3,4]. Reveal 1, bury 2 -> [3,4,2]. Reveal 3, bury 4 -> [2,4]. Reveal 2, bury 4 -> [4]. Reveal 4. Revealed order: 1 3 2 4.

ans.pattern: Simulation with a queue (deque)
ans.brute: Directly model the deck; each card is revealed or buried a bounded number of times.
ans.opt: Load 1..N into a queue. While non-empty: pop front and append to the output; if the queue is still non-empty, pop the next front and push it to the back. The output list is the reveal order.

e3.title: Round-Robin Scheduler
e3.story:
An operating system runs N processes, numbered 0 to N-1, on a single CPU using round-robin scheduling. Process i needs a known amount of CPU time (its burst) to finish. The scheduler keeps a ready queue that initially holds the processes in index order 0, 1, ..., N-1.

Repeatedly, the scheduler takes the process at the FRONT of the queue and runs it for a time slice of at most Q units: if the process needs Q or fewer units, it runs to completion this slice; otherwise it runs for exactly Q units, Q is subtracted from its remaining burst, and it goes to the BACK of the queue to wait its next turn. A process that completes leaves the system.

You must report the order in which processes COMPLETE (not the order they started). All bursts are positive, so every process eventually finishes.

Report the process indices in the order they complete, space-separated.
inf: First line: two integers N Q
Second line: N integers, the bursts in index order
outf: A single line: the process indices in completion order, space-separated
e3.exp: Queue [0,1,2], bursts [5,2,6], Q=3. P0 runs 3 (rem 2) -> back: [1,2,0]. P1 runs 2, completes -> order [1]; queue [2,0]. P2 runs 3 (rem 3) -> back: [0,2]. P0 runs 2, completes -> order [1,0]; queue [2]. P2 runs 3, completes -> order [1,0,2]. Output: 1 0 2.

ans.pattern: Simulation with a queue (round-robin)
ans.brute: Model the ready queue directly; each process cycles through until its burst is exhausted.
ans.opt: Load process indices into a queue with a remaining-burst array. Pop the front, run min(Q, remaining); if it finishes append it to the completion order, else decrement and requeue. Continue until the queue empties.
ans.cx: O(sum(burst)/Q) slices; fine for the given limits.

e4.title: Balanced Mobile
e4.story:
A hanging mobile is a binary structure of N nodes. Each node is either a LEAF holding a weight, or an INTERNAL node from which exactly two sub-mobiles hang, a left and a right. The TOTAL WEIGHT of a leaf is its own weight; the total weight of an internal node is the sum of the total weights of its two hanging sub-mobiles.

An internal node is BALANCED when the total weight hanging on its left equals the total weight hanging on its right -- the arm hangs level. Leaves are never called balanced or unbalanced; only internal nodes are judged.

You are given every node with its role. Internal-node references always point to other listed nodes, and following them from the root reaches every node without cycles.

Report how many internal nodes are balanced.
cons: internal references are valid node ids forming a tree from the root
inf: First line: integer N
Second line: the root node id
Next N lines: node i is either 'L w' (leaf of weight w) or 'I l r' (internal with children l, r)
outf: A single integer: the number of balanced internal nodes
e4.exp: Node2=5, Node4=2, Node5=3, so Node3 (internal over 4,5) has left 2 vs right 3 -> not balanced; Node1 (internal over 2,3) has left 5 vs right 5 -> balanced. Exactly 1 balanced internal node.

ans.pattern: Recursion (post-order totals, test balance on the way up)
ans.brute: One recursive pass computes every total once; recomputation would be exponential.
ans.opt: Recurse: a leaf returns its weight; an internal node computes left and right totals, increments the balanced count when they are equal, and returns their sum. The count after the traversal is the answer.

e5.title: Tallest Lineage
e5.story:
A royal family tree has N members, numbered 1 to N. Each member lists a parent (the monarch, the root, lists parent 0) and carries a personal 'renown' value. Following parents always reaches the root, and a member may have any number of children.

A LINEAGE is a path that starts at the monarch (the root) and walks down through children, one at a time, until it reaches a member with no children (a leaf). The renown of a lineage is the sum of the renown values of every member along that path, monarch and leaf included.

The historians want the single most renowned lineage: among all root-to-leaf paths, the maximum total renown. A tie in totals does not matter -- only the maximum value is needed.

Report the maximum lineage renown.
inf: First line: integer N
Next N lines: two integers renown parent for member i (1-indexed)
outf: A single integer: the maximum root-to-leaf renown sum
e5.exp: Root 1 (renown 10) has children 2 (5) and 3 (20); member 2 has child 4 (3). Path 1->3 totals 10+20=30; path 1->2->4 totals 10+5+3=18. The maximum lineage renown is 30.

ans.pattern: Recursion (max over children, plus own value)
ans.brute: Enumerating all root-to-leaf paths can be exponential in a bushy tree; recursion computes each subtree's best once.
ans.opt: best(node) = value(node) if it is a leaf, else value(node) + max(best(child)) over its children. Answer is best(root).

e6.title: Expression Tree
e6.story:
A calculator stores an arithmetic expression as a tree of N nodes. Each node is either a NUMBER leaf holding an integer value, or an OPERATOR node holding either '+' or '*' together with references to its two child nodes (its two operands). The value of a number node is its integer; the value of an operator node is its operator applied to the values of its two children.

Evaluation is recursive: to evaluate an operator node you must first evaluate both of its child subtrees, then combine them with the node's operator. Operator references always point to listed nodes and following them from the root reaches every node without cycles, so evaluation always terminates.

The values involved stay within normal 64-bit range for the given limits.

Report the value of the whole expression -- that is, the value of the root node.
cons: operator is '+' or '*'; child references form a tree from the root
inf: First line: integer N
Second line: the root node id
Next N lines: node i is either 'N v' (number v) or 'O op l r' (operator op with children l, r)
outf: A single integer: the value of the expression
e6.exp: Node3 is (Node4 * Node5) = 2 * 3 = 6. Node1 is (Node2 + Node3) = 4 + 6 = 10. The expression evaluates to 10.

ans.pattern: Recursion (post-order evaluation)
ans.brute: The value of a node depends on its children, so evaluate bottom-up; each node is evaluated once.
ans.opt: ev(node): if it is a number, return its value; otherwise evaluate both children and combine with '+' or '*'. Return ev(root).

e7.title: Friend Circles
e7.story:
A class has N students, numbered 0 to N-1. You are given an N by N friendship matrix: entry (i, j) is 1 if student i and student j are direct friends, and 0 otherwise. Friendship is mutual, so the matrix is symmetric, and every student is trivially listed as their own friend on the diagonal.

Friendship forms CIRCLES by transitivity: if A is a direct friend of B and B of C, then A, B and C all belong to the same friend circle even if A and C are not direct friends. A student with no friends other than themselves forms a circle of one.

The teacher wants to know how many distinct friend circles the class splits into.

Report the number of friend circles.
cons: matrix entries are 0 or 1; the matrix is symmetric with 1s on the diagonal
inf: First line: integer N
Next N lines: N integers each, the friendship matrix rows
outf: A single integer: the number of friend circles
e7.exp: Students 0 and 1 are direct friends -> one circle {0,1}; student 2 is friends with no one else -> circle {2}. Total 2 circles.

ans.pattern: Union-Find (DSU) over the adjacency matrix
ans.brute: A DFS/BFS over the matrix also works; DSU unions each friendship and counts roots.
ans.opt: Union i and j whenever entry (i,j) is 1 (upper triangle suffices). The number of distinct roots among the N students is the number of circles.

e8.title: Equation Consistency
e8.story:
A logic checker is given N unknowns, numbered 0 to N-1, and M constraints about them. Each constraint compares two unknowns and is one of two kinds: an EQUALITY saying two unknowns must hold the same value, or an INEQUALITY saying two unknowns must hold DIFFERENT values.

The checker must decide whether ALL M constraints can be satisfied simultaneously by some assignment of values to the unknowns. Equality is transitive -- if a equals b and b equals c, then a equals c must hold -- so equalities knit unknowns into groups that must share one value. An inequality is violated only if it demands two unknowns differ that the equalities have forced into the same group.

Constraints may be given in any order, and equalities and inequalities may be interleaved.

Print YES if every constraint can be satisfied at once, otherwise NO.
cons: each constraint is 'a b 1' (a==b) or 'a b 0' (a!=b), 0 <= a,b < N
inf: First line: two integers N M
Next M lines: three integers a b e (e=1 means a==b, e=0 means a!=b)
outf: YES if all constraints are satisfiable, otherwise NO
e8.exp: Equalities 0==1 and 1==2 force {0,1,2} into one group that must share a value. The inequality 0!=2 then demands two members of that same group differ, which is impossible. Answer NO.

ans.pattern: Union-Find (DSU): union all equalities first, then verify inequalities
ans.brute: Order matters only in that all equalities must be merged before inequalities are checked.
ans.opt: First union every '==' pair. Then for every '!=' pair, if the two unknowns share a root the constraints conflict -> NO. If none conflict -> YES.

e9.title: Fair Chocolate Split
e9.story:
A chocolate bar is a single row of N chunks, chunk i having a known sweetness. You will break the bar into exactly K+1 CONTIGUOUS pieces (making K breaks between adjacent chunks) and hand the pieces out to yourself and K friends -- one contiguous piece each. A piece's sweetness is the sum of its chunks' sweetness values, and every chunk must belong to exactly one piece.

Being generous, you always keep the LEAST sweet piece for yourself. So among the K+1 pieces, your share is whichever piece has the smallest total. You want to break the bar so that this minimum piece is as LARGE as possible -- maximising the worst piece.

Whether a target minimum m is achievable is monotone: if you can carve K+1 pieces each of sweetness at least m, you can certainly do it for any smaller m.

Report the largest achievable value of the minimum piece's sweetness.
inf: First line: two integers N K
Second line: N integers, the chunk sweetness in order
outf: A single integer: the maximum achievable minimum-piece sweetness
e9.exp: You must form K+1 = 6 contiguous pieces. Carving pieces whose sums are each at least 6 is possible (e.g. [1,2,3],[4,5]... wait totals) -- a feasibility scan shows the largest achievable minimum piece is 6.

ans.pattern: Binary search on the answer (greedy piece-count feasibility)
ans.brute: Trying every threshold is O(sum*N); binary search cuts the threshold dimension to log.
ans.opt: Binary-search the target minimum m. Greedily sweep, closing a piece each time the running sum reaches m; count how many pieces form. Feasible iff at least K+1 pieces can each reach m. The largest feasible m is the answer.

e10.title: Cookie Sharing
e10.story:
A volunteer has a bag of cookies of various sizes and a group of children, each child with a GREED FACTOR -- the minimum cookie size that will satisfy them. A child is content only if given a single cookie whose size is at least their greed factor, and each cookie can go to at most one child, each child gets at most one cookie.

The volunteer wants to make as MANY children content as possible. There are more or fewer cookies than children in general, and a cookie too small for a picky child might still satisfy a less demanding one, so matching greedily from the least demanding child upward, using the smallest cookie that still works, maximises the count.

Cookies left over or children left unserved are simply that -- the goal is only to maximise the number of content children.

Report the maximum number of content children.
inf: First line: two integers (number of children) (number of cookies)
Second line: the children's greed factors
Third line: the cookie sizes
outf: A single integer: the maximum number of content children
e10.exp: Sort greed [1,2,3] and cookies [1,1]. The first cookie (1) satisfies the child with greed 1; the second cookie (1) cannot satisfy greed 2 or 3. Only 1 child is content.

ans.pattern: Greedy (sort both, two-pointer match)
ans.brute: Trying assignments is combinatorial; sorting and matching smallest-fit is optimal.
ans.opt: Sort greeds and cookies. Walk a pointer through each: if the current cookie satisfies the current child, count it and advance both; otherwise advance only the cookie pointer. The count is the answer.

e11.title: Night Watch Loot
e11.story:
A row of N houses lines a street, house i holding a known amount of loot. A burglar plans one night's route but faces a strict alarm rule: robbing two DIRECTLY ADJACENT houses on the same night trips a shared alarm between them. So the burglar may rob any set of houses as long as no two chosen houses are next to each other.

The burglar wants to maximise the total loot taken under this no-two-adjacent rule. Skipping a rich house may be worth it if it unlocks two even richer non-adjacent ones, so a simple 'take every other house' rule is not optimal.

Houses hold non-negative loot, and the burglar may rob zero houses (taking 0), though with positive loot somewhere that is never best.

Report the maximum loot obtainable without robbing two adjacent houses.
inf: First line: integer N
Second line: N integers, the loot per house
outf: A single integer: the maximum non-adjacent loot
e11.exp: Choosing houses 0, 2 and 4 (loot 2, 9, 1) gives 12, and no valid selection beats it (e.g. 7+9 is adjacent and disallowed; 7+3+? cannot reach 12). Answer 12.

ans.pattern: Dynamic programming (include/exclude running totals)
ans.brute: The choice at each house depends only on the two running totals; no need to enumerate subsets.
ans.opt: Track inc = best total ending with this house robbed, exc = best total with it skipped. Transition: new inc = old exc + loot, new exc = max(old inc, old exc). Answer max(inc, exc).

e12.title: Shared Storyline
e12.story:
Two editors each trimmed the same manuscript differently, producing two strings A and B of scene codes. To measure how much of the original narrative survives in both, they want the length of the longest COMMON SUBSEQUENCE: the longest sequence of scene codes that appears in both A and B in the same relative order, though not necessarily contiguously.

A subsequence is formed by deleting zero or more characters from a string without reordering the rest. The common subsequence need not be a contiguous run in either editor's version -- scenes may be spread out -- but the order must be consistent with both.

Both strings are lowercase letters and may have different lengths. If they share no scene code at all, the answer is 0.

Report the length of the longest common subsequence of A and B.
cons: A and B are lowercase letters
inf: First line: string A
Second line: string B
outf: A single integer: the length of the longest common subsequence
e12.exp: The subsequence 'ace' appears in both 'abcde' (positions 0,2,4) and 'ace' (all), in order, and no common subsequence is longer. Answer 3.

ans.pattern: Dynamic programming (LCS table)
ans.brute: Enumerating subsequences is exponential; the 2-D prefix DP is polynomial.
ans.opt: dp[i][j] = LCS length of A's first i and B's first j characters. If the current characters match, dp[i][j]=dp[i-1][j-1]+1; otherwise max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]). Answer dp[|A|][|B|].

e13.title: Balance Point
e13.story:
A tightrope of N pegs holds a weight on each peg, given in order. An engineer wants a BALANCE POINT: an index i such that the total weight strictly to the LEFT of peg i equals the total weight strictly to the RIGHT of peg i. The weight on peg i itself is the pivot and counts toward neither side.

If several balance points exist, the engineer wants the SMALLEST index that works. The leftmost peg has nothing to its left (left sum 0) and the rightmost has nothing to its right (right sum 0), and either can be a valid balance point if the other side sums to zero.

Weights may be zero (some pegs are empty). If no index balances the two sides, report -1.

Report the smallest balance-point index, or -1 if none exists.
inf: First line: integer N
Second line: N integers, the peg weights
outf: A single integer: the smallest balance-point index, or -1
e13.exp: At index 2 (weight 5), the left sum is 1+3=4 and the right sum is 2+2=4 -- they match. No smaller index balances, so the answer is 2.

ans.pattern: Prefix sum (running left vs total-minus-left)
ans.brute: Recomputing both side-sums per index is O(N^2); a running left-sum with the precomputed total is linear.
ans.opt: Precompute the total. Sweep, keeping the running left sum; at index i the right sum is total - left - a[i]. Return the first i where left equals that right sum, else -1.

e14.title: Banner Repaint
e14.story:
A banner is a row of coloured tiles encoded as a string S of uppercase letters, one letter per colour. A decorator may REPAINT at most K tiles, each to any colour of their choosing, and wants the longest possible run of tiles that all share one colour AFTER repainting.

Concretely, find the length of the longest CONTIGUOUS window of the banner in which, by repainting at most K tiles, every tile in the window can be made the same colour. Within any window, the cheapest way to unify it is to keep the most frequent colour already present and repaint the rest, so a window of length W with its most frequent colour appearing F times needs W - F repaints, which must not exceed K.

The window must be contiguous; the decorator cannot skip tiles in the middle. K may be 0 (no repaints allowed).

Report the length of the longest achievable single-colour run after at most K repaints.
cons: S consists of uppercase English letters
inf: First line: the string S
Second line: integer K
outf: A single integer: the longest achievable single-colour run
e14.exp: The window 'AABA' (or 'ABBA') has 3 of its majority colour and length 4, needing only 1 repaint, which K=1 allows. No valid window of length 5 exists, so the answer is 4.

ans.pattern: Sliding window (window length minus max in-window frequency <= K)
ans.brute: Checking every window is O(N^2 * 26); a sliding window keeping colour counts is linear.
ans.opt: Expand the right end, updating colour counts and the max frequency seen. While (window length - max frequency) exceeds K, shrink from the left. Track the largest valid window width.

e15.title: Stone Smash
e15.story:
A pile has N stones of given integer weights. A machine repeatedly smashes the two HEAVIEST stones together. If the two heaviest weigh x and y with x >= y, then: if x equals y both stones are destroyed; otherwise both are destroyed and a new stone of weight x - y is dropped back into the pile. Smashing continues as long as at least two stones remain.

At the end there is either one stone left or none. The operator wants the weight of that last remaining stone, or 0 if every stone was destroyed. Because the two heaviest change after each smash (a newly created stone may itself become the heaviest), the pile must be re-examined for the top two each round.

Report the weight of the last remaining stone, or 0 if none remain.
inf: First line: integer N
Second line: N integers, the stone weights
outf: A single integer: the weight of the last stone, or 0
e15.exp: Smash 8,7 -> 1 back (pile 2,4,1,1,1). Smash 4,2 -> 2 (pile 2,1,1,1). Smash 2,1 -> 1 (pile 1,1,1). Smash 1,1 -> destroyed (pile 1). One stone of weight 1 remains.

ans.pattern: Heap / priority queue (max-heap of weights)
ans.brute: Re-sorting to find the top two each round is O(N^2 log N); a max-heap gives them in log time.
ans.opt: Use a max-heap. Each round pop the two largest; if they differ push their difference. When fewer than two remain, output the last stone's weight or 0.

e16.title: Knight's Errand
e16.story:
A lone knight stands at the origin (0, 0) of an effectively unbounded chessboard and must reach a target square at coordinates (tx, ty). The knight moves as in chess: each move jumps to one of eight squares that are two steps in one axis and one step in the perpendicular axis (for example +1 in x and +2 in y).

The knight wants to reach the target in the FEWEST moves. Because the board is huge, the knight can freely roam into negative coordinates and around the target if that helps a shortest tour, but an optimal route never needs to wander far beyond the target.

Every move is equally costly, so this is a shortest-path count in an unweighted movement graph. The target is always reachable by a knight.

Report the minimum number of knight moves from (0, 0) to (tx, ty).
inf: A single line: two integers tx ty
outf: A single integer: the minimum number of knight moves
e16.exp: A single knight move from (0,0) lands on (2,1) directly, so the minimum is 1 move.

ans.pattern: Graph: breadth-first search over knight moves
ans.brute: DFS would not give the fewest moves; BFS explores by move-count layers, bounded to a region around the target.
ans.opt: BFS from (0,0) generating the 8 knight moves, within a bounding box a little larger than the target, marking visited squares. The depth when the target is dequeued is the answer.

e17.title: Least Strenuous Trail
e17.story:
A hiker crosses a terrain grid of R rows by C columns, where each cell has an integer elevation. The hiker starts at the top-left cell and must reach the bottom-right cell, moving one cell at a time up, down, left or right (never diagonally, never off the grid).

The STRAIN of a route is the largest single step it makes -- that is, the maximum over all consecutive cells on the route of the absolute difference in their elevations. A route with one brutal cliff is worse than a longer route that only ever steps gently, even if the gentle route visits more cells.

The hiker wants the route whose strain is as SMALL as possible: minimise the maximum elevation change between consecutive cells along the way.

Report the minimum possible strain of a route from the top-left to the bottom-right cell.
inf: First line: two integers R C
Next R lines: C integers, the elevation grid
outf: A single integer: the minimum possible strain
e17.exp: Following the route 1->2->2->2->3->5 down the right side and along the bottom keeps every step's elevation change at most 2, and no route can guarantee a smaller maximum step. The minimum strain is 2.

ans.pattern: Graph: Dijkstra variant (minimise the maximum edge along a path)
ans.brute: Binary-search + BFS also works; Dijkstra where a path's cost is the max edge (not the sum) finds it directly.
ans.opt: Run Dijkstra but define the cost to reach a cell as the minimum over paths of the largest single step. Relax a neighbour with max(currentEffort, |elevation difference|); pop by smallest effort. The effort at the destination is the answer.

e18.title: Reservoir Walls
e18.story:
A row of N vertical walls stands along a base line, wall i having a given height and each pair of adjacent walls one unit apart. Choosing any TWO walls as the sides of a reservoir, the water it can hold is limited by the shorter of the two walls (water would spill over it) times the horizontal distance between them.

Formally, for walls at positions i and j the volume is (j - i) multiplied by the minimum of the two heights. The engineer wants to pick the two walls that maximise this volume -- the widest, tallest effective container -- ignoring any walls in between (assume they do not obstruct).

Walls may repeat in height, and the best pair is not always the two tallest walls, since distance matters too.

Report the maximum volume of water any pair of walls can hold.
inf: First line: integer N
Second line: N integers, the wall heights
outf: A single integer: the maximum water volume
e18.exp: The walls of height 8 (index 1) and 7 (index 8) span distance 7 and are limited by the shorter height 7, holding 7*7 = 49 -- the maximum over all pairs.

ans.pattern: Two pointers (converge from both ends)
ans.brute: Checking all O(N^2) pairs is too slow; two pointers moving inward from the widest span is linear.
ans.opt: Start pointers at both ends. Compute the volume; then move the pointer at the SHORTER wall inward (the only move that can find a taller limiting wall). Track the maximum volume seen.

f1.title: Crane Restacking
f1.story:
A dockyard has C storage columns in a row, numbered 0 to C-1; column j starts with a known number of stacked boxes. A gantry crane then performs K moves in order. Each move names a source column and a destination column, and the crane lifts the SINGLE top box off the source and drops it on top of the destination.

There is one catch the operators keep forgetting: if the source column is EMPTY when its move comes up, the crane has nothing to lift and the move is simply skipped, changing nothing. A move whose source and destination are the same column also leaves heights unchanged.

After all K moves, the yard manager wants the height of the TALLEST column, to check no column has grown past the crane's safe reach.

Report the maximum column height after all moves.
inf: First line: two integers C K
Second line: C integers, the starting column heights
Next K lines: two integers a b, move the top box of column a onto column b
outf: A single integer: the tallest column height after all moves
f1.exp: Start [2,0,1]. Move 0->1: [1,1,1]. Move 0->2: [0,1,2]. Move 2->1: [0,2,1]. Tallest column holds 2 boxes.

ans.pattern: Simulation (apply each move to a heights array)
ans.brute: There is no shortcut; apply moves in order, guarding against an empty source.
ans.opt: Keep an array of heights. For each move, if the source is non-empty, decrement it and increment the destination. Report the maximum height at the end.

f2.title: Rotated Panel
f2.story:
A square control panel is an N by N grid of integer codes. A technician rotates the WHOLE panel 90 degrees CLOCKWISE exactly once: the top row becomes the right column, the right column becomes the bottom row, and so on. After the rotation, the operator reads the code sitting at a particular cell, given by its row and column (0-indexed) in the ROTATED panel.

Rotating a grid 90 degrees clockwise sends the cell originally at row i, column j to row j, column (N-1-i). Equivalently, the value now at rotated cell (r, c) is the value that was originally at row (N-1-c), column r.

You are given the original panel and one query cell in the rotated panel.

Report the code at the queried cell of the rotated panel.
inf: First line: three integers N qr qc
Next N lines: N integers each, the original panel
outf: A single integer: the code at rotated cell (qr, qc)
f2.exp: Rotated 90 clockwise the panel becomes rows [7,4,1],[8,5,2],[9,6,3]. Cell (0,2) holds 1, which is the original top-left value.

ans.pattern: Simulation (index arithmetic of a 90-degree rotation)
ans.brute: You need not materialise the whole rotation; the queried value is a direct index map.
ans.opt: The rotated cell (r, c) equals the original cell (N-1-c, r). Read that single value (or rotate the whole grid if you prefer).
ans.cx: O(1) per query (O(N^2) to read input).

f3.title: Two-Teller Bank
f3.story:
A bank has exactly two tellers and a single ordered line of N customers; customer i is given by an arrival time and a service duration, and the customers are listed in non-decreasing arrival order. A teller serves one customer at a time and never interrupts a service.

When a customer reaches the front, they go to whichever teller becomes free EARLIEST; if both tellers are free at the same moment, the customer picks teller 0 (the lower-numbered one). If the chosen teller is free before the customer arrives, service starts at the arrival time; otherwise the customer waits and service starts the instant that teller frees up. Service then runs for the customer's full duration.

The manager wants to know when the bank can finally close: the finishing time of the LAST customer to be done (which is not necessarily the last customer in line, since the two tellers run in parallel).

Report the time at which the final service completes.
inf: First line: integer N
Next N lines: two integers arrival duration for customer i (in arrival order)
outf: A single integer: the completion time of the last-finishing service
f3.exp: Customer0 (arr0,dur4) -> teller0, ends at 4. Customer1 (arr1,dur3) -> teller1 free at 0, starts at 1, ends 4. Customer2 (arr2,dur2) -> both free at 4, picks teller0, starts 4, ends 6. Last completion is 6.

ans.pattern: Simulation (assign each customer to the earlier-free teller)
ans.brute: Just track two teller free-times and process customers in order.
ans.opt: Keep free[0], free[1]. For each customer choose the teller with the smaller free time (ties -> teller 0); start = max(arrival, that free time); update it to start+duration. The answer is the maximum completion time.

f4.title: Bracket Repair
f4.story:
A configuration file uses only round brackets '(' and ')' to mark nested blocks, but a faulty editor has left the string UNBALANCED. You must compute the minimum number of bracket characters to INSERT (anywhere in the string) so that it becomes balanced -- every '(' has a matching ')' after it and every ')' has a matching '(' before it, properly nested.

You may only insert brackets; you cannot delete or reorder the existing ones. A ')' that appears with no unmatched '(' before it needs a '(' inserted to its left; any '(' left unmatched at the end needs a ')' inserted to its right.

An already-balanced string needs 0 insertions.

Report the minimum number of insertions to balance the string.
inf: A single line: the bracket string S
outf: A single integer: the minimum number of insertions
f4.exp: Reading '(', '(', ')': the first ')' matches one open bracket, leaving one '(' still open at the end. That single unmatched '(' needs one ')' inserted. Answer 1.

ans.pattern: Simulation (running count of unmatched open brackets)
ans.brute: A stack works but a single counter suffices.
ans.opt: Track open = unmatched '(' so far. On '(' increment; on ')' decrement if open>0 else count one insertion (a needed '('). At the end, add the remaining open (needed ')'). Sum is the answer.

f5.title: Org Chart Reach
f5.story:
A company org chart has N employees, numbered 1 to N. Each employee lists their direct manager; exactly one employee is the CEO and lists manager 0. Following managers always reaches the CEO, and an employee may have any number of direct reports.

An employee's REACH is the total number of people beneath them in the hierarchy -- all their direct reports, plus those people's reports, and so on, all the way down (but NOT counting the employee themselves). The CEO's reach is everyone else; a leaf employee with no reports has reach 0.

HR wants to find the single largest span of control in the company: the maximum reach over all employees.

Report the maximum reach.
inf: First line: integer N
Next N lines: the manager of employee i (0 for the CEO), one per line
outf: A single integer: the maximum reach over all employees
f5.exp: Employee 1 is CEO with reports 2 and 3; employee 2 has report 4. Subtree sizes: emp1=4, emp2=2, emp3=1, emp4=1. Reach = size - 1: emp1=3, emp2=1, others 0. Maximum reach is 3.

ans.pattern: Recursion (subtree sizes)
ans.brute: One post-order pass computes every subtree size once.
ans.opt: size(i) = 1 + sum(size(child)). The reach of i is size(i)-1; track the maximum reach while recursing.

f6.title: Hierarchy Depth
f6.story:
A file system is described as a tree of N folders, numbered 1 to N. Each folder lists its parent folder; the single top folder (the drive root) lists parent 0, and following parents always reaches it. A folder may contain any number of sub-folders.

The DEPTH of the tree is the length, measured in EDGES (parent-child links), of the longest path from the root down to any folder that has no sub-folders. The root alone (with no sub-folders) has depth 0; a root with a child but no grandchildren has depth 1.

An indexing tool needs this depth to size its traversal stack.

Report the depth of the folder tree in edges.
inf: First line: integer N
Next N lines: the parent of folder i (0 for the root), one per line
outf: A single integer: the tree depth in edges
f6.exp: Root 1 has children 2 and 3; folder 2 has child 4. The longest root-to-leaf path is 1 -> 2 -> 4, which is 2 edges. Depth is 2.

ans.pattern: Recursion (height of each subtree)
ans.brute: One post-order pass; a leaf has height 0.
ans.opt: height(i) = 0 if i has no children, else 1 + max(height(child)). Return height(root).

f7.title: Even Wards
f7.story:
A kingdom's territory is a tree of N regions, numbered 1 to N. Each region has a population and a parent region (the capital, the root, lists parent 0); following parents always reaches the capital. A region may have any number of sub-regions.

For each region, define its DOMAIN POPULATION as the sum of its own population plus the populations of every region beneath it in the tree (its whole subtree). The census office wants to count how many regions have an EVEN domain population.

A leaf region's domain population is just its own population; the capital's domain population is the whole kingdom.

Report the number of regions whose domain population is even.
inf: First line: integer N
Next N lines: two integers population parent for region i (parent 0 marks the capital)
outf: A single integer: the count of regions with an even domain population
f7.exp: Domain populations: region4=4, region2=2+4=6, region3=3, region1=1+6+3=10. Even ones are region4 (4), region2 (6) and region1 (10) -> 3 regions.

ans.pattern: Recursion (subtree sums, test parity on the way up)
ans.brute: One post-order pass computes each subtree sum once.
ans.opt: subtreeSum(i) = population[i] + sum(subtreeSum(children)); increment a counter whenever a subtree sum is even. Return the count.

f8.title: Toll Grid
f8.story:
A delivery drone crosses a city modelled as an R by C grid of blocks; every block charges a non-negative toll to fly over it, paid each time the drone is on that block, including the start block and the destination block. The drone starts at the top-left block and must reach the bottom-right block.

To save battery the drone only ever flies one block RIGHT or one block DOWN at a time -- never up or left. Among all such monotone routes, it wants the one whose total toll paid is the smallest.

Unlike some versions there are no blocked blocks here; every block is passable, and a valid route always exists.

Report the minimum total toll of a route from the top-left to the bottom-right block.
inf: First line: two integers R C
Next R lines: C integers, the toll grid
outf: A single integer: the minimum total toll
f8.exp: The route right,right,down,down collects 1+3+1+1+1 = 7; the down-first route collects 1+1+4+2+1 = 9. The minimum is 7.

ans.pattern: Dynamic programming (grid prefix minima)
ans.brute: Enumerating all monotone routes is exponential; the DP reuses each cell's best once.
ans.opt: dp[i][j] = toll[i][j] + min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]) (with the top row and left column accumulating in one direction). Answer dp[R-1][C-1].

f9.title: Cipher Decode
f9.story:
A message was encoded by mapping letters to numbers -- 'A' to 1, 'B' to 2, ..., 'Z' to 26 -- and then writing those numbers with no separators, producing a string of digits S. A codebreaker wants to know how many DIFFERENT original letter strings could have produced S.

At each position the decoder may read a single digit (1-9) as one letter, or two adjacent digits as one letter if they form a number from 10 to 26. A leading zero is never valid: '0' cannot start a letter, and a two-digit group like '07' is not a valid letter either, so some strings decode in zero ways.

Because the count can be large, report it modulo 1000000007.

Report the number of distinct decodings of S modulo 1000000007.
inf: A single line: the digit string S
outf: A single integer: the number of decodings modulo 1000000007

ans.pattern: Dynamic programming (Fibonacci-like over positions)
ans.brute: Trying every split is exponential; each position's count depends only on the previous one or two.
ans.opt: dp[i] = ways to decode the first i digits. dp[i] += dp[i-1] if digit i is 1-9; dp[i] += dp[i-2] if the two digits ending at i form 10-26. Handle leading zeros as zero ways.

f10.title: Longest Mirror
f10.story:
A biologist scans a DNA-like string S of letters and wants the longest CONTIGUOUS stretch that reads the same forwards and backwards -- a palindrome. Such symmetric stretches mark structurally interesting regions.

The stretch must be contiguous (a substring, not a subsequence): you cannot delete letters from the middle. A palindrome may have even or odd length; a single letter is trivially a palindrome of length 1, so the answer is at least 1 for any non-empty string.

Among all palindromic substrings, you only need the LENGTH of the longest one, not the substring itself. If several tie for longest, the length is the same for all.

Report the length of the longest palindromic substring of S.
cons: S consists of lowercase English letters
inf: A single line: the string S
outf: A single integer: the length of the longest palindromic substring
f10.exp: 'bab' and 'aba' are both palindromic substrings of length 3, and no palindromic substring is longer, so the answer is 3.

ans.pattern: Dynamic programming / expand-around-centre
ans.brute: Checking every substring for palindromicity is O(N^3); centre expansion (or an interval DP) is O(N^2).
ans.opt: For each of the 2N-1 possible centres (each letter and each gap), expand outward while the characters match, tracking the longest span found.

f11.title: Minimum Cable Plan
f11.story:
A campus must connect N buildings, numbered 1 to N, with network cable. There are M possible cable runs; run i connects two buildings and has a known installation cost. The IT team wants to choose a set of runs so that every building is connected (directly or through others) into a single network, while paying the LEAST total installation cost.

This is a minimum spanning selection: pick runs of least total cost that tie all buildings together without needing any redundant loop. Adding a run that connects two already-connected buildings only wastes money.

If the available runs cannot connect all buildings into one network (some building is isolated no matter what), the plan is impossible.

Report the minimum total cost to connect all buildings, or -1 if it cannot be done.
cons: cable runs are two-way; 1 <= u, v <= N
inf: First line: two integers N M
Next M lines: three integers u v w (a run between u and v costing w)
outf: A single integer: the minimum total connection cost, or -1
f11.exp: Sorting runs by cost and adding those that join new buildings: take 1-2 (1), 2-3 (2), 3-4 (3); all four buildings are now connected for a total of 6. The 1-4 run (4) would form a redundant loop and is skipped.
