ans.pattern: Union-Find (DSU) with Kruskal's algorithm
ans.brute: Trying subsets of runs is exponential; Kruskal greedily adds the cheapest safe run.
ans.opt: Sort runs by cost. Scan them; add a run (and its cost) only if its endpoints are in different DSU components, then union them. If fewer than N-1 runs are added, the graph is disconnected -> -1.

f12.title: Extra Wire
f12.story:
A technician wired up N sensors that were supposed to form a tree -- exactly N-1 wires connecting all N sensors with no loops. By mistake one EXTRA wire was added, so there are N wires in total and they now contain exactly one cycle. The sensors are numbered 1 to N and there are N wires listed in the order they were installed.

The technician wants to identify the redundant wire whose removal restores a proper tree: specifically, among the wires that lie on the cycle, the one that appears LAST in the installation order. Removing it leaves all N sensors connected with no loop.

Equivalently, process the wires in order and find the first wire whose two endpoints are ALREADY connected by earlier wires -- that wire is the one that closes the cycle.

Report the redundant wire as its two endpoints, in the order they are given.
cons: exactly N wires; the graph has exactly one cycle
inf: First line: integer N (the number of sensors, equal to the number of wires)
Next N lines: two integers a b, a wire (in installation order)
outf: A single line: the two endpoints of the redundant wire, space-separated
f12.exp: Wires 1-2 and 1-3 connect all three sensors. The wire 2-3 joins two sensors already connected (through sensor 1), closing the cycle, so it is the redundant wire.

ans.pattern: Union-Find (DSU): the redundant edge joins an already-connected pair
ans.brute: Detecting the cycle by repeated graph search is slower; DSU spots the closing edge in one pass.
ans.opt: Process wires in order. For each, if its endpoints share a DSU root it is the redundant wire (remember it); otherwise union them. The last such wire found is the answer (here there is exactly one).

f13.title: Two-Crop Row
f13.story:
A long orchard row has N trees, each of a single fruit type given as an integer. A picker walks a CONTIGUOUS stretch of the row carrying just two baskets, and each basket can hold only one fruit type. So along any stretch the picker walks, the trees may use at most TWO distinct fruit types in total.

The picker wants the LONGEST contiguous stretch of trees that uses at most two distinct fruit types, to maximise the harvest in one walk. The stretch must be contiguous -- the picker cannot skip a tree of a third type in the middle and continue.

A row using only one or two types overall means the whole row qualifies. Fruit types can repeat anywhere.

Report the length of the longest contiguous stretch containing at most two distinct fruit types.
inf: First line: integer N
Second line: N integers, the fruit type of each tree in order
outf: A single integer: the longest stretch with at most 2 distinct types
f13.exp: The stretch [1,2,1,2] uses two types and has length 4. Extending to include the 3 would make three distinct types, so 4 is the longest.

ans.pattern: Sliding window (shrink when distinct types exceed 2)
ans.brute: Checking all substrings is O(N^2); a window with a type-count map is linear.
ans.opt: Expand the right edge, counting types in a map. While the map holds more than two distinct types, advance the left edge, removing types as their counts hit zero. Track the widest window.

f14.title: Cheap Baskets
f14.story:
A shop lists N items in a row, item i priced at a positive integer. A 'cheap basket' is any CONTIGUOUS run of items whose prices MULTIPLIED together come out strictly less than a budget K. The manager wants to count how many cheap baskets exist.

Every contiguous run counts as its own basket, so runs covering different positions are counted separately even if they contain the same prices. A single item whose price is already at least K forms no cheap basket on its own, and if K is 1 or less nothing qualifies.

Because all prices are positive, extending a run only multiplies its product up, never down -- the property that lets a forward-moving window count baskets efficiently.

Report the number of contiguous runs whose price product is strictly less than K.
inf: First line: two integers N K
Second line: N integers, the item prices in order
outf: A single integer: the number of contiguous runs with product < K
f14.exp: Sliding a window keeping the product under 100: each new right end contributes (window length) new baskets ending there. Summing gives 8 cheap baskets in total.

ans.pattern: Sliding window (product, all-positive)
ans.brute: Enumerating every run and multiplying is O(N^2); a window keeps a running product in linear time.
ans.opt: Grow the window on the right, multiplying the running product. While the product is >= K, divide out the left element and advance the left edge. Each step adds (right-left+1) new qualifying runs ending at the right.

f15.title: Bloom Day
f15.story:
A florist has a garden row of N flowers; flower i blooms on a specific day (given) and, once bloomed, stays bloomed. The florist needs to assemble exactly M bouquets, and each bouquet requires K ADJACENT flowers that have all bloomed -- the K flowers of a bouquet must be consecutive in the row, and a flower can be used in at most one bouquet.

Waiting more days means more flowers have bloomed, making bouquets easier to form; so the question is the EARLIEST day on which the florist can gather all M bouquets at once. Whether a given day works is monotone: if day d suffices, so does any later day.

If the garden simply does not have enough flowers (M times K exceeds N), it can never be done.

Report the minimum day on which M bouquets can be made, or -1 if it is impossible.
inf: First line: three integers N M K
Second line: N integers, the bloom day of each flower in row order
outf: A single integer: the earliest feasible day, or -1
f15.exp: With K=1 each bloomed flower is its own bouquet. By day 3, flowers with bloom days 1, 3 and 2 have opened -- three flowers, enough for 3 bouquets. Day 2 yields only two. So the earliest day is 3.

ans.pattern: Binary search on the answer (greedy bouquet count)
ans.brute: Trying every day is too slow; the feasibility is monotone in the day, so binary-search it.
ans.opt: Binary-search the day. For a candidate day, sweep the row counting runs of consecutive bloomed flowers; each run of length L yields floor(L/K) bouquets. Feasible if the total reaches M. Smallest feasible day wins.

j1.title: Sunlit Nodes
j1.story:
A tree of N observation posts (numbered 1 to N) is planted on a hillside; each post has a height and a parent post it was built after, with the single base post (the root) listing parent 0. Following parents always reaches the base, and a post may have any number of children.

A post is called SUNLIT if its height is STRICTLY greater than the height of every post on the path from the base down to it, not counting itself (all of its strict ancestors). The base post has no ancestors, so it is always sunlit. A post tied with its tallest ancestor is NOT sunlit, since the rule is strict.

The survey wants the total number of sunlit posts.

Report the count of sunlit posts.
inf: First line: integer N
Next N lines: two integers height parent for post i (parent 0 marks the base)
outf: A single integer: the number of sunlit posts
j1.exp: Post1 (root, 3) is sunlit. Post2 (4) beats its only ancestor 3 -> sunlit. Post3 (2) does not beat ancestor 3 -> not sunlit. Post4 (5) beats ancestors 3 and 4 -> sunlit. Total 3.

ans.pattern: Recursion (carry the max ancestor height down)
ans.brute: Recomputing each post's ancestor maximum separately is wasteful; pass it down the DFS.
ans.opt: DFS from the root carrying the maximum height seen among strict ancestors. A post is sunlit if its height exceeds that maximum; recurse into children with the updated maximum.

j2.title: Even Split
j2.story:
A warehouse must divide N crates between two identical trucks so that both trucks carry the same total weight. Each crate has a positive integer weight and must go entirely on one truck or the other -- crates cannot be split.

The dispatcher wants to know whether such a perfectly equal division is even possible. If the total weight of all crates is odd, it clearly cannot be halved. If it is even, the question becomes whether some subset of crates sums to exactly half the total (the rest then form the other half).

This is not always achievable even when the total is even -- it depends on the particular weights.

Print YES if the crates can be split into two equal-weight groups, otherwise NO.
inf: First line: integer N
Second line: N integers, the crate weights
outf: YES if an equal split exists, otherwise NO
j2.exp: Total is 22, half is 11. The subset {11} sums to 11 and the rest {1,5,5} also sum to 11, so an equal split exists -> YES.

ans.pattern: Dynamic programming (subset-sum to half the total)
ans.brute: Trying all 2^N subsets is exponential; the boolean subset-sum DP is pseudo-polynomial.
ans.opt: If the total is odd, answer NO. Otherwise fill a boolean dp where dp[c] means some subset sums to c; for each weight update capacities downward. Answer YES iff dp[total/2] is reachable.

j3.title: Smallest Divisor
j3.story:
A batch process must divide each of N job sizes by a single chosen positive integer D and round each result UP to the next whole number (ceiling), then sum those rounded values. The sum represents total machine passes, and it must not exceed a threshold H.

A larger divisor D makes each ceiling smaller, so the total sum falls as D grows; a smaller D makes the sum larger. The operator wants the SMALLEST divisor D for which the summed passes stay within the threshold H, because a small divisor keeps each pass finer-grained.

The sum is a non-increasing function of D, which is the structure to exploit. A divisor of at least 1 always works in the limit (the sum never needs D beyond the largest job size).

Report the smallest divisor D whose ceiling-sum is at most H.
inf: First line: two integers N H
Second line: N integers, the job sizes
outf: A single integer: the smallest valid divisor
j3.exp: With D=5: ceil(1/5)+ceil(2/5)+ceil(5/5)+ceil(9/5) = 1+1+1+2 = 5 <= 6, valid. With D=4: 1+1+2+3 = 7 > 6, invalid. So the smallest valid divisor is 5.

ans.pattern: Binary search on the answer
ans.brute: Trying every divisor is O(maxSize * N); the monotone sum lets you binary-search the divisor.
ans.opt: Binary-search D in [1, max job]. For each D compute the ceiling-sum; feasible if it is <= H. The sum decreases as D grows, so the smallest feasible D is the answer.

j4.title: Clear the Schedule
j4.story:
A shared lab receives N reservation requests for one day; request i runs from start s_i to end e_i, treated as the half-open interval [s_i, e_i) so a request may start exactly when another ends without conflict. Because the lab has only one bench, no two accepted reservations may overlap in time.

The coordinator will CANCEL as few requests as possible so that the remaining reservations are all mutually non-overlapping. Equivalently, keep the largest possible set of compatible reservations and cancel the rest.

Requests arrive unsorted and can overlap in any pattern -- nested, chained, or staggered. A reservation ending exactly when the next begins does not overlap it.

Report the minimum number of reservations that must be cancelled.
inf: First line: integer N
Next N lines: two integers s e, a reservation
outf: A single integer: the minimum number of cancellations
j4.exp: Sorted by end: (1,2),(2,3),(1,3),(3,4). Keep (1,2); (2,3) starts at 2 -> keep; (1,3) starts at 1 < 3 -> conflicts, cancel; (3,4) starts at 3 -> keep. One cancellation.

ans.pattern: Greedy (keep the most non-overlapping intervals, sort by end)
ans.brute: Trying subsets is exponential; the earliest-end-first rule maximises the kept set.
ans.opt: Sort by end time. Sweep keeping a reservation only if its start is at or after the last kept end; count the kept ones. Cancellations = N - kept.

j5.title: Two-City Interviews
j5.story:
A company must fly exactly 2N candidates to interviews, sending precisely N to city A and precisely N to city B. Candidate i has a known cost to fly to city A and a known cost to fly to city B; the two costs differ per candidate. The recruiter wants to assign each candidate to exactly one city so that exactly half go to each city and the TOTAL travel cost is minimised.

The catch is the balance constraint: simply sending each candidate to their personally cheaper city could overfill one city. The right idea is to consider how much MORE a candidate costs for A versus B and send to A those for whom choosing A saves the most (or costs the least extra).

Every candidate must be assigned, and the two cities must end with equal counts.

Report the minimum total travel cost.
inf: First line: the integer 2N (the number of candidates, which is even)
Next 2N lines: two integers costA costB for each candidate
outf: A single integer: the minimum total travel cost
j5.exp: Sort by (costA - costB): candidate2 (-170), candidate0 (-10), candidate3 (+10), candidate1 (+350). Send the first two to A (30+10... i.e. 30 and 10) and the last two to B (20 and 50). Total 30+10+20+50 = 110.

ans.pattern: Greedy (sort by the A-minus-B cost difference)
ans.brute: Trying all balanced assignments is combinatorial; sorting by the cost difference is optimal.
ans.opt: Sort candidates by (costA - costB) ascending. Send the first N (who benefit most from A) to city A and the remaining N to city B; sum the chosen costs.

j6.title: Rooftop Runner
j6.story:
A courier crosses N buildings in a row, running left to right; building i has a known height. To step from one building to the next, if the next building is the same height or shorter, the step is free. If the next building is TALLER, the courier must bridge the height difference either by laying down bricks (using exactly that many bricks) or by placing one ladder (a ladder covers any single climb regardless of size).

The courier carries a limited number of bricks and a limited number of ladders. Ladders are precious, so they are best saved for the LARGEST climbs, while bricks handle the smaller ones. The courier wants to reach as far as possible before running out of both.

The courier stops just before the first climb they can neither brick nor ladder.

Report the index (0-based) of the FURTHEST building the courier can reach.
inf: First line: three integers N bricks ladders
Second line: N integers, the building heights
outf: A single integer: the index of the furthest reachable building
j6.exp: Climbs occur at 2->7 (5) and 6->9 (3) and 9->14 (5). Keeping the one ladder for a size-5 climb and paying bricks for the others, the 5 bricks run out at the second big climb, stranding the courier at index 4.

ans.pattern: Heap / priority queue (assign ladders to the largest climbs)
ans.brute: Trying every ladder assignment is exponential; a min-heap of climbs so far lets you always brick the smallest.
ans.opt: Walk the buildings; for each positive climb push it on a min-heap. While the heap holds more climbs than ladders, spend bricks on the smallest climb (pop it). If bricks go negative, the current building index is the furthest reached.

j7.title: Cooldown Scheduler
j7.story:
A CPU must run a sequence of tasks given as a string of uppercase letters, where each letter is a task type. Each time unit the CPU either runs one task or stays idle. The catch is a COOLDOWN: after running a task of a given type, at least N time units must pass before another task of the SAME type can run. Different task types have no cooldown between them.

You may run the tasks in ANY order (the letters just tell you how many of each type there are). The scheduler wants to finish all tasks in the FEWEST total time units, inserting idle slots only when forced by the cooldown rule.

The bottleneck is the most frequent task type: its copies must be spread at least N+1 apart, and other tasks (or idles) fill the gaps.

Report the minimum total time units to run all tasks.
inf: First line: the task string
Second line: the cooldown N
outf: A single integer: the minimum total time units
j7.exp: With cooldown 2, an optimal order is A B _ A B _ A B, taking 8 time units (one forced idle after each of the first two A-B pairs is avoided by interleaving; the frame formula gives (3-1)*(2+1)+2 = 8).

ans.pattern: Greedy / heap (frame around the most frequent task)
ans.brute: Simulating with a heap of remaining counts works; the closed-form frame formula is O(1) after counting.
ans.opt: Let f = highest task frequency and c = how many types share it. The answer is max(totalTasks, (f-1)*(N+1) + c): the frames formed by the most frequent task, or the task count if there are enough distinct tasks to avoid idling.

j8.title: Cheapest Layover
j8.story:
An airline network has N airports (0 to N-1) connected by M one-way flights, each with a price. A traveller wants the cheapest itinerary from a source airport to a destination airport, but with a comfort limit: they will tolerate at most K STOPS in between (a stop is an intermediate airport, so K stops means at most K+1 flights).

Among all itineraries from source to destination using at most K stops, the traveller wants the minimum total price. Some itineraries with more stops might be cheaper but are not allowed; the stop limit is a hard cap.

Some destinations may be unreachable within the stop limit at all. Flights are one-way and there may be several flights between the same pair with different prices.

Report the minimum total price within at most K stops, or -1 if the destination is unreachable under the limit.
inf: First line: two integers N M
Second line: three integers source destination K
Next M lines: three integers u v w (a flight u->v priced w)
outf: A single integer: the cheapest price within K stops, or -1
j8.exp: With at most 1 stop: the direct flight 0->2 costs 500, while 0->1->2 (one stop) costs 100+100 = 200. The cheaper allowed itinerary is 200.

ans.pattern: Bellman-Ford limited to K+1 relaxation rounds (a Dijkstra-on-(node,stops) state also works)
ans.brute: Plain Dijkstra ignores the stop cap; you must bound the number of edges used.
ans.opt: Relax all edges exactly K+1 times, each round working from the PREVIOUS round's distances (so each round adds at most one more flight). After K+1 rounds, dist[destination] is the cheapest within K stops, or -1 if still infinite.

j9.title: Marsh Crossing
j9.story:
A ranger crosses a marsh modelled as an R by C grid; standing on cell (i,j) costs a known amount of energy, paid each time the ranger enters it, including the start and end cells. Unlike a simple downhill trek, the ranger may move in ANY of the four orthogonal directions -- up, down, left, or right -- to route around expensive bog cells.

The ranger starts at the top-left cell and must reach the bottom-right cell while spending the LEAST total energy. Because movement is four-directional, a cheapest route may weave up and left, not just down and right, so a simple row-by-row pass is not enough.

All cell costs are non-negative, so no route benefits from looping.

Report the minimum total energy to cross from the top-left to the bottom-right cell.
inf: First line: two integers R C
Next R lines: C integers, the energy cost grid
outf: A single integer: the minimum total energy
j9.exp: A cheapest route runs right,right,down,down collecting 1+3+1+1+1 = 7; weaving through the high-cost centre or bottom-left costs more. The minimum energy is 7.

ans.pattern: Graph: Dijkstra on grid cells (4-directional)
ans.brute: Four-directional movement can require going up/left, so a DP pass is insufficient; Dijkstra handles it.
ans.opt: Dijkstra from the top-left with distance = accumulated cell cost, relaxing all four neighbours. The finalised distance at the bottom-right is the answer.

j10.title: Clear Corridor
j10.story:
A rescue drone must cross a square N by N grid where each cell is either clear (0) or blocked (1). The drone starts at the top-left cell and must reach the bottom-right cell. Unusually, it may move to any of the EIGHT surrounding cells -- horizontally, vertically, or diagonally -- as long as the target cell is clear and on the grid.

The path length is counted as the number of CELLS visited along the route, including both the start and the end cell. The drone wants the shortest such path.

If the start or the end cell is blocked, or no clear 8-connected route exists between them, the crossing is impossible.

Report the length (in cells) of the shortest clear path from the top-left to the bottom-right, or -1 if none exists.
inf: First line: integer N
Next N lines: N integers each (0 or 1), the grid
outf: A single integer: the shortest path length in cells, or -1
j10.exp: Moving right along the top row then down the right column (with a diagonal where possible), a shortest clear 8-connected route visits 4 cells: (0,0),(0,1) or a diagonal,...,(2,2). The answer is 4.

ans.pattern: Graph: breadth-first search (8-connected grid)
ans.brute: DFS gives a path but not the shortest; BFS explores by cell-distance layers.
ans.opt: BFS from the top-left over clear cells using all 8 neighbours, counting cells (start = 1). The count when the bottom-right is reached is the answer; -1 if start/end blocked or unreachable.

j11.title: Portal Hops
j11.story:
A player stands on the first of N pads laid in a row, numbered 0 to N-1; each pad shows a coloured rune (an integer). From the pad at index i, in a single hop the player may move to index i-1, to index i+1, or teleport to ANY other pad that shows the SAME rune as pad i -- all of these count as one hop.

The player wants to reach the last pad (index N-1) in the FEWEST hops. Because same-rune pads can be scattered anywhere, a single hop can leap across the whole row, so the shortest route is not obvious.

Once the player has used the teleport network for a given rune, those same-rune pads need not be re-scanned (they are all reachable in one hop from the first time that rune is touched).

Report the minimum number of hops to reach the last pad.
inf: First line: integer N
Second line: N integers, the rune on each pad
outf: A single integer: the minimum number of hops to the last pad
j11.exp: Hop from index 0 (rune 100) to index 4 (same rune 100), then to index 3 (rune 404) via neighbour... an optimal route reaches the last pad in 3 hops.

ans.pattern: Graph: breadth-first search with value buckets
ans.brute: Naively re-scanning same-value pads each visit is O(N^2); clearing a bucket after first use keeps it linear.
ans.opt: BFS from index 0. Neighbours of i are i-1, i+1, and every not-yet-visited index sharing a[i]'s value; after expanding a value's bucket, empty it so it is never scanned again. The depth at index N-1 is the answer.

j12.title: Divisible Spans
j12.story:
A logistics ledger has N signed daily adjustments. Auditors want to count how many CONTIGUOUS spans of days have a total adjustment that is divisible by a modulus K (a span-sum of 0 counts as divisible by K). Spans covering different day ranges are counted separately even if their sums match.

The span must be contiguous; you cannot drop a day in the middle. Because adjustments can be negative, the running total is not monotone, so a shrinking-window approach does not apply -- but two prefix totals that leave the SAME remainder modulo K bound a span whose sum is divisible by K.

Remainders must be taken carefully so that negative running totals map to a remainder in the range 0 to K-1.

Report the number of contiguous spans whose sum is divisible by K.
inf: First line: two integers N K
Second line: N integers, the daily adjustments
outf: A single integer: the number of spans with sum divisible by K
j12.exp: Grouping prefix sums by remainder mod 5 and counting equal-remainder pairs (plus prefixes that are themselves 0 mod 5) yields 7 divisible spans.

ans.pattern: Prefix sum modulo K + frequency map
ans.brute: Checking every span is O(N^2); equal prefix remainders mark divisible spans.
ans.opt: Track the running prefix sum modulo K (normalised to 0..K-1) and a count of each remainder seen (seed remainder 0 with count 1). For each new prefix remainder, add how many times it has occurred, then record it.

j13.title: Parallel Semesters
j13.story:
A curriculum has N courses (0 to N-1) and M prerequisite rules; a rule 'a b' means course a must be completed before course b. A student can take ANY number of courses in the same semester, as long as all prerequisites of each chosen course were completed in earlier semesters.

The student wants to graduate in the FEWEST semesters. Each semester they take every course whose prerequisites are already all done. The number of semesters is therefore the number of dependency 'layers' in the prerequisite graph.

If the prerequisites contain a cycle, the courses can never all be completed. Otherwise every course fits into some layer.

Report the minimum number of semesters to complete all courses, or -1 if impossible.
inf: First line: two integers N M
Next M lines: two integers a b (a before b)
outf: A single integer: the minimum number of semesters, or -1
j13.exp: Semester 1: course 0 (no prereqs). Semester 2: courses 1 and 2 (prereq 0 done). Semester 3: course 3 (prereqs 1 and 2 done). Three semesters.

ans.pattern: Graph: topological sort processed in BFS layers (Kahn)
ans.brute: The answer is the number of Kahn layers; a plain topological order alone does not give it.
ans.opt: Kahn's algorithm layer by layer: start with all zero-in-degree courses as layer 1, remove them, and whatever becomes zero-in-degree forms the next layer. Count layers; if not all courses are processed, a cycle exists -> -1.

j14.title: Skyline Billboard
j14.story:
A row of N adjacent buildings each has a given height and unit width, forming a skyline. An advertiser wants to hang the largest possible RECTANGULAR billboard flush against the buildings: the rectangle sits on the ground and its height is limited by the SHORTEST building it spans, while its width is the number of consecutive buildings it covers.

Formally, for any contiguous range of buildings the billboard area is (number of buildings in the range) multiplied by (minimum height in the range). The advertiser wants the maximum such area over all contiguous ranges.

A single tall building can beat a wide short span, or vice versa, so both dimensions must be balanced.

Report the maximum billboard area.
inf: First line: integer N
Second line: N integers, the building heights
outf: A single integer: the maximum rectangle area
j14.exp: The two buildings of heights 5 and 6 give a 2-wide rectangle of height 5 = area 10, which is the maximum over all contiguous spans.

ans.pattern: Monotonic stack (each bar as the limiting height)
ans.brute: Trying every range and finding its minimum is O(N^2); a monotonic stack finds each bar's span in amortised O(1).
ans.opt: Keep a stack of indices with non-decreasing heights. When a shorter bar appears, pop taller bars and, for each popped bar, compute the area with it as the limiting height over the span between the new bar and the previous stacked bar. A sentinel 0 at the end flushes the stack.

j15.title: Rainwater Basins
j15.story:
After a storm, water collects between the columns of a bar chart. You are given N bar heights in a row; each bar has unit width. Water is trapped above a bar up to the level of the shorter of the tallest bars to its left and to its right; any water above that level spills away.

Formally, the water held above bar i is max(0, min(highest bar to the left including i, highest bar to the right including i) - height of bar i). The total trapped water is the sum of this over all bars.

Bars at the very ends and local peaks hold no water; only dips flanked by taller bars on both sides do.

Report the total units of trapped rainwater.
inf: First line: integer N
Second line: N integers, the bar heights
outf: A single integer: the total trapped water
j15.exp: Summing the water held above each dip (bounded by the taller walls on each side) gives 6 units of trapped rainwater for this profile.

ans.pattern: Two pointers (converging, tracking left and right maxima)
ans.brute: Precomputing left/right maxima uses O(N) extra space; two pointers do it in O(1) space.
ans.opt: Place pointers at both ends with running left-max and right-max. Advance the side with the smaller height, adding (that side's running max - current height) to the total, since that side's bound is confirmed by the taller opposite wall.

k1.title: Conveyor Offset
k1.story:
A circular conveyor holds N trays in fixed slots numbered 0 to N-1. Overnight the belt is rotated LEFT by K positions: after one left rotation the tray in slot 1 moves to slot 0, the tray in slot 0 wraps around to slot N-1, and so on. After K such left rotations the operator reads the tray now sitting in slot P.

A left rotation by K sends the tray originally in slot (P+K) mod N into slot P. So rather than physically rotating, you can compute directly which original tray ends up under any given slot.

K can be larger than N (the belt may spin many full turns), which is why the wrap-around modulo matters.

Report the tray value now in slot P after K left rotations.
inf: First line: three integers N K P
Second line: N integers, the tray values in slot order
outf: A single integer: the value in slot P after K left rotations
k1.exp: After 2 left rotations the array reads 30,40,50,10,20. Slot 1 holds 40, which is the original slot (1+2) mod 5 = 3 value.

ans.pattern: Simulation (direct index arithmetic of rotation)
ans.brute: No need to rotate the array K times; the mapping is a single modulo.
ans.opt: The value at slot P after K left rotations is the original value at index (P+K) mod N.

k2.title: Bracket Score
k2.story:
A scoring language uses only balanced round brackets, and a valid balanced string is scored by three rules applied recursively: the empty pair '()' scores 1; two balanced strings written next to each other, A followed by B, score the sum of their scores; and a balanced string A wrapped in a pair, written (A), scores twice the score of A.

You are given one guaranteed-balanced bracket string and must compute its total score under these rules. The nesting can be deep and the concatenations many, so the score builds up from the innermost pairs outward.

Report the score of the bracket string.
cons: S is a balanced string of only '(' and ')'
inf: A single line: the balanced bracket string S
outf: A single integer: the score of S
k2.exp: Innermost pairs score 1 each. Working outward, (()(())) evaluates to 2*( 1 + 2*1 ) = 2*3 = 6.

ans.pattern: Simulation with a stack of running scores
ans.brute: The score depends only on nesting; a stack accumulates each level's score.
ans.opt: Push 0 on '('; on ')' pop the level's value v and add max(2*v, 1) to the new top (max handles an empty pair scoring 1). The bottom of the stack holds the final score.

k3.title: Backspace Length
k3.story:
A minimal text editor processes a stream of keystrokes given as a string. Every ordinary character is typed and appended to the document, but the special character '#' represents a BACKSPACE, which deletes the most recently typed character still present. A backspace pressed when the document is already empty simply does nothing.

After processing the entire keystroke stream in order, the editor wants the LENGTH of the resulting document (the number of characters that remain).

Report the length of the final document.
cons: S consists of lowercase letters and the character '#'
inf: A single line: the keystroke string S
outf: A single integer: the length of the final document
k3.exp: Type 'a', type 'b', backspace removes 'b' leaving 'a', type 'c' giving 'ac'. The final length is 2.

ans.pattern: Simulation with a stack
ans.brute: Process keystrokes with a stack; a backspace pops if non-empty.
ans.opt: Push each ordinary character; on '#' pop one character if the stack is non-empty. The final stack size is the answer.

k4.title: Spiral Pick
k4.story:
A museum lays out N by C exhibit tiles as an R by C grid of exhibit codes. A guided tour walks them in a clockwise inward SPIRAL: along the top row left to right, down the right column, along the bottom row right to left, up the left column, then spiralling inward one ring at a time until every tile is visited.

The guide wants to know which exhibit code is the K-th tile visited on this spiral tour (counting from 1 at the top-left starting tile).

Report the exhibit code at the K-th position of the spiral order.
inf: First line: three integers R C K
Next R lines: C integers each, the grid
outf: A single integer: the K-th code in spiral order
k4.exp: The spiral order is 1,2,3,6,9,8,7,4,5. The 5th tile visited holds 9.

ans.pattern: Simulation (spiral boundary traversal)
ans.brute: Walk the four shrinking boundaries, collecting cells until the K-th.
ans.opt: Maintain top/bottom/left/right boundaries; append the top row, right column, bottom row and left column in turn, shrinking each after its pass. Return the K-th collected value.

k5.title: Team Importance
k5.story:
A company org chart has N employees, numbered 1 to N; each has an importance score and a direct manager (the CEO lists manager 0). Following managers always reaches the CEO, and an employee may have any number of direct reports.

For a given employee Q, the manager wants the TOTAL importance of Q's team: Q's own importance plus the importance of every employee beneath Q in the hierarchy (all reports, their reports, and so on).

Report the total importance of the subtree rooted at employee Q.
inf: First line: two integers N Q
Next N lines: two integers importance manager for employee i (manager 0 marks the CEO)
outf: A single integer: the total importance of Q's team
k5.exp: Employee 1 is the CEO with reports 2 (importance 3) and 3 (importance 2). Q=1's team importance is 5+3+2 = 10.

ans.pattern: Recursion (subtree sum from Q)
ans.brute: One DFS from Q sums its whole subtree.
ans.opt: Build children lists. sum(i) = importance[i] + sum over children of sum(child). Return sum(Q).

k6.title: Landmark Peaks
k6.story:
A trail network is a tree of N viewpoints, numbered 1 to N; each has an elevation and a parent viewpoint (the trailhead, the root, lists parent 0). Following parents always reaches the trailhead.

A viewpoint is a LANDMARK if its elevation is at least as high as every viewpoint on the path from the trailhead down to it (all of its ancestors) -- in other words, nothing before it on the way up was taller. The trailhead itself is always a landmark. Note the comparison is 'at least' (>=), so a viewpoint tied with the tallest ancestor still counts.

Report the number of landmark viewpoints.
inf: First line: integer N
Next N lines: two integers elevation parent for viewpoint i (parent 0 marks the trailhead)
outf: A single integer: the number of landmark viewpoints
k6.exp: Trailhead 1 (3) is a landmark. Node2 (1) < 3, not. Node3 (4) >= 3, landmark. Node4 (1) < 4, not. Node5 (5) >= 4, landmark. Total 3.

ans.pattern: Recursion (carry the max ancestor elevation)
ans.brute: Pass the running maximum down the DFS instead of recomputing ancestry.
ans.opt: DFS from the root with the maximum elevation among ancestors; a node is a landmark if its elevation is >= that maximum. Recurse with the updated maximum.

k7.title: Quest Routes
k7.story:
A dungeon is laid out as a tree of N rooms, numbered 1 to N; each room holds a treasure value and lists a parent room (the entrance, the root, lists parent 0). Following parents always reaches the entrance, and a room may branch into any number of sub-rooms.

A COMPLETE RUN is a path that starts at the entrance and descends through sub-rooms until it reaches a room with no sub-rooms (a dead end). The loot of a run is the sum of the treasure values along that path, entrance and dead end included.

The guild wants to know how many complete runs have loot EXACTLY equal to a target T.

Report the number of entrance-to-dead-end runs whose loot equals T.
inf: First line: two integers N T
Next N lines: two integers treasure parent for room i (parent 0 marks the entrance)
outf: A single integer: the number of complete runs with loot exactly T
k7.exp: Runs: entrance1->2->4 loots 5+4+2 = 11; entrance1->3 loots 5+8 = 13. Only the first equals T=11, so the count is 1.

ans.pattern: Recursion (accumulate path sum, test at leaves)
ans.brute: One DFS carrying the running path sum; check it only at dead ends.
ans.opt: DFS from the root adding each room's treasure to a running sum; at a leaf, if the sum equals T increment the count. Return the count.

k8.title: Stair Toll
k8.story:
A staircase has N steps, and stepping onto step i costs a known toll. A climber may start from either step 0 or step 1 (paying that step's toll), and from any step may move up one or two steps at a time. The 'top' is the imaginary landing just beyond the last step; reaching it costs nothing extra.

The climber wants to reach the top paying the LEAST total toll. Because a cheap step now can force an expensive step later, a simple greedy choice is not safe.

Report the minimum total toll to reach the top.
inf: First line: integer N
Second line: N integers, the toll on each step
outf: A single integer: the minimum toll to reach the top
k8.exp: Start on step 1 (toll 15) and step two up to the top, skipping step 2's toll of 20. Total 15, which beats starting on step 0.

ans.pattern: Dynamic programming (reach-cost of each step)
ans.brute: The cost to stand on a step depends only on the previous two; a rolling DP suffices.
ans.opt: dp[i] = toll[i] + min(dp[i-1], dp[i-2]). The answer is min(dp[N-1], dp[N-2]) since the top is reachable from either of the last two steps.

k9.title: Best Product Run
k9.story:
A factory records the daily performance MULTIPLIER of a process for N days; each day's value is an integer that may be positive, negative, or zero. Analysts want the largest product obtainable from a CONTIGUOUS run of days -- the days multiplied together.

The run must be contiguous and contain at least one day. The tricky part is negatives: two negatives multiply to a positive, so a very negative day can suddenly become valuable when paired with another negative later, while a zero resets any running product.

Report the maximum product of any contiguous run of days.
inf: First line: integer N
Second line: N integers, the daily multipliers
outf: A single integer: the maximum contiguous product
k9.exp: The run [2,3] gives 6; extending past -2 turns negative, and [4] alone is 4. The maximum contiguous product is 6.

ans.pattern: Dynamic programming (track running max AND min products)
ans.brute: A single running max fails on negatives; you must also carry the running minimum (most negative), which a negative can flip to a maximum.
ans.opt: For each value keep the max and min product of a run ending here, each chosen from {value, value*prevMax, value*prevMin}. Track the global maximum.

k10.title: Grid Routes
k10.story:
A robot starts at the top-left cell of an R by C grid and must reach the bottom-right cell, moving only one cell RIGHT or one cell DOWN at a time. Every cell is open (there are no obstacles). The control software wants to know how many DISTINCT monotone routes exist from the start to the destination.

Because the count can be enormous for large grids, report it modulo 1000000007.

Report the number of distinct right/down routes modulo 1000000007.
inf: First line: two integers R C
outf: A single integer: the number of routes modulo 1000000007
k10.exp: On a 3 by 3 grid there are 6 distinct right/down routes from the top-left to the bottom-right cell.

ans.pattern: Dynamic programming (grid path counts) or a binomial coefficient
ans.brute: Enumerating routes is exponential; the count of paths to a cell is the sum of the cell above and the cell to the left.
ans.opt: dp[j] over one row, initialised to 1s (top row); for each subsequent row update dp[j] += dp[j-1]. The last cell holds the count. (Equivalently C(R+C-2, R-1).)

k11.title: Sensor Clusters
k11.story:
A field has N sensors, numbered 0 to N-1, and M wireless links; each link lets two sensors talk directly, and communication is transitive (linked sensors and everyone they reach form one cluster). A sensor with no links is a cluster of one.

The operations team wants to know into how many separate CLUSTERS the sensors fall after all M links are accounted for. Duplicate links and self-links may appear and do not change the clustering.

Report the number of connected clusters.
inf: First line: two integers N M
Next M lines: two integers a b, a link
outf: A single integer: the number of clusters
k11.exp: Links merge {0,1,2} and {3,4}; there is no fifth-cluster sensor here since all five are placed, giving clusters {0,1,2} and {3,4} -> 2 clusters.

ans.pattern: Union-Find (DSU)
ans.brute: A BFS/DFS component count also works; DSU unions each link and counts distinct roots.
ans.opt: Union every link; the number of distinct roots over all N sensors is the cluster count.

k12.title: Loop Detector
k12.story:
A plumbing network has N junctions, numbered 0 to N-1, connected by M two-way pipes. The inspector wants to know whether the pipes contain a LOOP -- a cycle where you can leave a junction and return to it through distinct pipes without backtracking.

Equivalently, as pipes are added one by one, a loop is formed the first time a pipe connects two junctions that are ALREADY connected through earlier pipes.

Print YES if the network contains at least one loop, otherwise NO.
inf: First line: two integers N M
Next M lines: two integers a b, a pipe
outf: YES if a cycle exists, otherwise NO
k12.exp: Pipes 0-1 and 1-2 connect all three junctions; the pipe 2-0 then joins two already-connected junctions, closing a loop. Answer YES.

ans.pattern: Union-Find (DSU): a cycle appears when an edge joins an already-connected pair
ans.brute: Repeated graph traversal is slower; DSU spots the closing edge in one pass.
ans.opt: For each pipe, if its endpoints already share a DSU root a cycle exists; otherwise union them. If no such edge appears, there is no cycle.

k13.title: Best K-Day Window
k13.story:
A weather station records a daily comfort score (which can be negative) for N consecutive days. A festival organiser will run the event for a block of EXACTLY K consecutive days and wants the block whose comfort scores sum to the largest total.

Across all contiguous K-day windows, find the maximum sum. The window must be exactly K days wide and contiguous.

Recomputing each window from scratch wastes work since neighbouring windows overlap in K-1 days; sliding the window is far faster.

Report the maximum sum over any K-consecutive-day window.
inf: First line: two integers N K
Second line: N integers, the daily comfort scores
outf: A single integer: the maximum K-day window sum
k13.exp: The K=4 window sums are 2, 51, 42. The window [12,-5,-6,50] sums to 51, the maximum.

ans.pattern: Sliding window (fixed size)
ans.brute: Summing each window in O(K) is O(N*K); the slide is linear.
ans.opt: Compute the first K-sum, then for each step add the entering day and subtract the leaving day, tracking the maximum window sum.

k14.title: Anagram Sweep
k14.story:
A security scanner has a short signature string P and a long log string T, both lowercase letters. It must decide whether ANY contiguous window of T is an ANAGRAM of P -- that is, some run of exactly |P| consecutive characters in T uses each letter the same number of times as P does (a rearrangement of P).

The window must be contiguous and exactly the length of P. Only the letter counts matter, not the order.

Print YES if such a window exists in T, otherwise NO.
cons: P and T are lowercase letters
inf: First line: the signature string P
Second line: the log string T
outf: YES if some window of T is an anagram of P, otherwise NO
k14.exp: The window 'ba' in T (positions 3-4) is a rearrangement of 'ab', so a matching window exists -> YES.

ans.pattern: Sliding window (fixed-size frequency match)
ans.brute: Re-counting each window is O(|T|*26); a sliding frequency count updates in O(1) per step.
ans.opt: Maintain a frequency count of the current |P|-length window of T and compare it to P's counts as the window slides one character at a time.

k15.title: Bus Fleet Trips
k15.story:
A depot runs N shuttle buses; bus i completes one round trip every per_i minutes, and buses run independently and continuously. The depot must complete a total of T round trips across the whole fleet (any bus's trips count toward the total) as quickly as possible.

In t minutes, bus i completes floor(t / per_i) trips, so the fleet's total in t minutes is the sum of those. More time means more trips, so the total is non-decreasing in t. The depot wants the SMALLEST number of minutes by which the fleet has completed at least T trips.

Report the minimum minutes needed to reach at least T total trips.
inf: First line: two integers N T
Second line: N integers, each bus's minutes per trip
outf: A single integer: the minimum minutes to reach T total trips
k15.exp: In 3 minutes the buses complete 3 + 1 + 1 = 5 trips, meeting T=5; in 2 minutes only 2 + 1 + 0 = 3 trips. So the minimum time is 3.

ans.pattern: Binary search on the answer
ans.brute: Trying every minute is too slow; the trip total is monotone in time, so binary-search the time.
ans.opt: Binary-search t in [1, min(per)*T]. The trips completed by time t is sum(t // per_i); the smallest t whose total is >= T is the answer.

p1.title: Sawmill Blade
p1.story:
A sawmill has a row of N trees of given heights and a blade set at some height H. When the blade sweeps across, it slices the top off every tree taller than H, collecting (tree height - H) units of wood from each such tree; trees at or below H are untouched and yield nothing.

The mill has an order for at least M units of wood. To leave the trees as tall as possible (for future harvests), the mill wants the HIGHEST blade setting H that still collects at least M units in this single sweep. A higher blade collects less wood, so the collected amount decreases as H rises -- the structure to exploit.

Report the maximum blade height H for which the harvested wood is at least M.
inf: First line: two integers N M
Second line: N integers, the tree heights
outf: A single integer: the maximum feasible blade height H
p1.exp: At H=15 the wood is (20-15)+(17-15) = 5+2 = 7, meeting M=7. At H=16 it is 4+1 = 5 < 7. So the highest valid blade is 15.

ans.pattern: Binary search on the answer
ans.brute: Trying every height is O(maxH * N); the wood total is monotone in H, so binary-search it.
ans.opt: Binary-search H in [0, max height]. For each H, harvested = sum(height - H) over taller trees; feasible if that is >= M. Take the largest feasible H.

p2.title: Truck Loadout
p2.story:
A delivery truck can carry at most T boxes total. There are several BOX TYPES; for each type you are told how many boxes of that type are available and how many units each box of that type holds. You may load any mix of boxes (up to the available count of each type) as long as the total number of boxes does not exceed T.

The dispatcher wants to maximise the total UNITS carried. Since every box takes exactly one of the T slots regardless of type, the best strategy is to fill slots with the highest-unit boxes first.

Report the maximum total units the truck can carry.
inf: First line: two integers (number of box types) T
Next lines: two integers count unitsPerBox for each type
outf: A single integer: the maximum total units
p2.exp: Fill by richest boxes: one box of 3 units (1 slot), two boxes of 2 units (2 slots), then one box of 1 unit (last slot). Units = 3 + 4 + 1 = 8.

ans.pattern: Greedy (take highest-unit boxes first)
ans.brute: Trying combinations is unnecessary; every box costs one slot, so richer boxes always win.
ans.opt: Sort box types by units per box descending. Fill slots greedily: take as many of the richest type as fit, then the next, until T slots are used or boxes run out.

p3.title: Label Partition
p3.story:
A ribbon is printed with a string of lowercase letters. It must be cut into the MAXIMUM number of contiguous pieces such that no letter appears in more than one piece -- every occurrence of any given letter must fall within a single piece.

Because a letter can appear far apart, a piece must stretch at least to the last occurrence of every letter it contains, which may pull in still more letters and extend it further. The goal is to make as MANY pieces as possible under this constraint.

Report the number of pieces in the maximal partition.
cons: S consists of lowercase English letters
inf: A single line: the string S
outf: A single integer: the maximum number of pieces
p3.exp: The first piece must extend to cover all of a,b,c -> 'ababcbaca'; the next covers d,e,f,g -> 'defegde'; the last covers h,i,j,k,l -> 'hijhklij'. Three pieces.

ans.pattern: Greedy (extend each piece to the last index of any letter inside it)
ans.brute: Precompute each letter's last index; a single sweep closes a piece when the scan reaches the running farthest last-index.
ans.opt: Record the last index of every letter. Sweep, tracking the farthest last-index among letters seen since the piece began; when the current position reaches that farthest index, close a piece and start a new one.

p4.title: Fuel Stops
p4.story:
A car must drive a straight highway of length TARGET, starting with startFuel units of fuel; one unit of fuel drives one unit of distance. Along the way are M fuel stations, station j positioned at a distance from the start and offering a fixed amount of fuel that can be pumped when the car reaches it (the tank is unlimited).

The car can only pump fuel at stations it actually reaches. The driver wants to arrive at TARGET using the FEWEST refuelling stops. The clever idea: drive as far as the current fuel allows, and whenever the car would run dry, retroactively 'use' the largest fuel station passed so far -- greedily taking big tanks first minimises the number of stops.

Report the minimum number of refuelling stops to reach the target, or -1 if it cannot be reached.
inf: First line: three integers TARGET startFuel M
Next M lines: two integers position fuel for each station
outf: A single integer: the minimum number of stops, or -1
p4.exp: Start with 10, reach station at 10 (bank 60 available). To go further, take the 60 (stop 1, fuel 60 -> reach 60), then take the 40 at position 60 (stop 2 -> reach 100+). Two stops suffice.

ans.pattern: Heap / priority queue (greedily use the largest passed tank)
ans.brute: Trying subsets of stations is exponential; a max-heap of passed-station fuels lets you always grab the biggest when needed.
ans.opt: Sweep stations in position order, pushing each reachable station's fuel to a max-heap. Whenever fuel is short of the next needed distance, pop the largest fuel and count a stop; if the heap is empty first, it is impossible.

p5.title: Streaming Median
p5.story:
Sensor readings arrive one at a time as a stream of N integers. After every reading, a dashboard must show the running MEDIAN of all readings seen so far. Because readings are integers and the display shows an integer, the median is defined as follows: with an odd count it is the middle value; with an even count it is the LOWER of the two middle values.

Re-sorting the whole history after each reading is far too slow for a long stream, so the median must be maintained incrementally as readings arrive.

After each of the N readings, report the running lower-median, space-separated in order.
inf: First line: integer N
Second line: N integers, the readings in arrival order
outf: A single line: the running lower-median after each reading, space-separated
p5.exp: After 5: median 5. After 15: {5,15} lower median 5. After 1: {1,5,15} median 5. After 3: {1,3,5,15} lower median 3. Output: 5 5 5 3.

ans.pattern: Heap / priority queue (max-heap of low half, min-heap of high half)
ans.brute: Re-sorting each step is O(N^2 log N); two balanced heaps keep the median at a heap top.
ans.opt: Keep a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half, rebalanced so the low half has equal or one more element. The lower median is the top of the max-heap after each insertion.

p6.title: Delivery Radius
p6.story:
A courier hub sits at node S of a network of N locations (1 to N) joined by M one-way roads, each with a positive travel time. For planning, the dispatcher wants the SUM of the shortest travel times from the hub S to every location reachable from it (the hub itself contributes 0, and unreachable locations contribute nothing).

This total 'delivery radius' summarises how far-flung the reachable network is. Roads are one-way with positive times, and there may be several roads between the same ordered pair.

Report the sum of shortest-path distances from S to all reachable locations.
inf: First line: two integers N M
Second line: the source S
Next M lines: three integers u v w (a road u->v with time w)
outf: A single integer: the sum of shortest distances to all reachable nodes
p6.exp: Shortest distances from 1: to 2 is 1, to 3 is min(4, 1+1)=2, to 4 is 2+2=4, and to itself 0. Their sum is 0+1+2+4 = 7.

ans.pattern: Graph: Dijkstra, then sum the finalised distances
ans.brute: Enumerating paths is exponential; Dijkstra finds every shortest distance in near-linear-log time.
ans.opt: Run Dijkstra from S. Sum the finalised distances of all reachable nodes (skip those left at infinity).

p7.title: Trailhead to Peak
p7.story:
A hiking map has N landmarks (1 to N) joined by M two-way trails, each with a positive walking time. A hiker wants the shortest total walking time from a trailhead landmark S to a peak landmark D, switching trails at intermediate landmarks as needed.

Trails are two-way and all times are positive, so a shortest route never revisits a landmark, but several routes may compete -- a chain of short trails can beat one long trail. Some landmarks may be unreachable from S.

Report the minimum walking time from S to D, or -1 if D cannot be reached.
inf: First line: two integers N M
Second line: two integers S D
Next M lines: three integers u v w (a two-way trail u-v with time w)
outf: A single integer: the shortest time from S to D, or -1
p7.exp: The route 1-2-3-4-5 costs 2+2+1+3 = 8, beating 1-3-5 (5+7=12) and 1-2-3-5 (2+2+7=11). The shortest time is 8.

ans.pattern: Graph: Dijkstra on an undirected weighted graph
ans.brute: Enumerating routes is exponential; Dijkstra with a heap handles positive weights efficiently.
ans.opt: Build an undirected adjacency list. Dijkstra from S; read off dist[D], or -1 if it stayed infinite.

p8.title: Farthest from Water
p8.story:
A map is an R by C grid where each cell is water (0) or land (1). For every land cell, its 'dryness' is the number of orthogonal steps to the NEAREST water cell (moving up, down, left, or right). The survey wants the maximum dryness over all land cells -- the land cell that is farthest from any water.

Water cells have dryness 0. It is guaranteed at least one water cell exists, so every land cell has a finite distance.

Report the maximum dryness among all cells.
cons: each cell is 0 (water) or 1 (land); at least one water cell exists
inf: First line: two integers R C
Next R lines: C integers (0 or 1)
outf: A single integer: the maximum distance from any cell to the nearest water
p8.exp: Running a multi-source BFS from all water cells, the land cell (2,1) is 2 steps from the nearest water; no land cell is farther. The maximum dryness is 2.

ans.pattern: Graph: multi-source BFS from all water cells
ans.brute: A per-cell BFS is O((RC)^2); one BFS seeded with every water cell labels all distances at once.
ans.opt: Seed the queue with all water cells at distance 0 and BFS outward, stamping each cell's nearest-water distance. The answer is the maximum stamp.

p9.title: Combination Lock
p9.story:
A padlock has four rotating wheels, each showing a digit 0-9 that wraps (9 turns to 0, 0 turns to 9). The lock starts at '0000'. In one move you rotate a SINGLE wheel one step, up or down. Certain 'dead' combinations jam the lock: if any wheel ever shows a dead combination the lock seizes, so you may never pass through one (and if the start itself is dead, you are stuck).

You want to reach a target combination in the FEWEST moves without ever landing on a dead combination.

Report the minimum number of moves to reach the target, or -1 if it is impossible.
inf: First line: the target combination
Second line: the number of deadends D
Next D lines: one deadend combination each
outf: A single integer: the minimum moves, or -1
p9.exp: A shortest safe sequence of single-wheel turns from 0000 to 0202, avoiding all five dead combinations, takes 6 moves.

ans.pattern: Graph: breadth-first search over lock states
ans.brute: Each of the 10000 states is a node with 8 neighbours; BFS finds the fewest moves.
ans.opt: BFS from '0000' (unless it is dead). Each state has 8 neighbours (each wheel +-1 with wrap); skip dead and visited states. The depth when the target is first reached is the answer.

p10.title: Range Audit
p10.story:
An auditor has an array of N daily figures and a list of Q audit queries. Each query names an inclusive range of days [l, r] (0-indexed) and asks for the sum of the figures over that range. Rather than reporting each query separately, the auditor wants the GRAND TOTAL: the sum of all Q query answers combined.

Answering each query by re-scanning its range would be too slow when both N and Q are large; a prefix-sum table answers each range in constant time.

Report the sum of the answers to all Q range queries.
inf: First line: two integers N Q
Second line: N integers, the daily figures
Next Q lines: two integers l r, an inclusive query range
outf: A single integer: the sum of all query answers

ans.pattern: Prefix sum (range sum in O(1))
ans.brute: Re-summing each range is O(N*Q); a prefix array makes each range O(1).
ans.opt: Build prefix sums pre where pre[i] is the sum of the first i figures. A query [l,r] equals pre[r+1]-pre[l]. Add up all query answers.

p11.title: Ordered Assembly
p11.story:
An assembly of N parts (0 to N-1) has M precedence rules; a rule 'a b' means part a must be installed before part b. The factory wants a single valid installation order of all N parts that respects every rule -- and, among all valid orders, the LEXICOGRAPHICALLY SMALLEST one (at each step, install the smallest-numbered part that is currently allowed).

If the rules contain a cycle, no valid order exists.

Report the lexicographically smallest valid order as space-separated part numbers, or -1 if none exists.
inf: First line: two integers N M
Next M lines: two integers a b (a before b)
outf: A single line: the lexicographically smallest topological order, or -1
p11.exp: Part 0 has no prerequisites (install first). Then among {1,2} pick the smaller, 1, then 2, then 3. The order is 0 1 2 3.

ans.pattern: Graph: topological sort (Kahn) with a min-heap for ties
ans.brute: A plain queue gives some valid order; a min-heap makes it the lexicographically smallest.
ans.opt: Kahn's algorithm but store zero-in-degree nodes in a min-heap; always pop the smallest available part, then release its successors. If fewer than N parts are emitted, a cycle exists -> -1.

p12.title: Safe Rooms
p12.story:
A dungeon has N rooms (0 to N-1) connected by M one-way passages. A room is a DEAD END if it has no outgoing passage. A room is SAFE if EVERY path leaving it is guaranteed to end at a dead end -- that is, no matter which passages you follow from it, you can never get caught in a cycle.

Rooms that can reach a cycle (or are part of one) are unsafe. Dead ends are trivially safe.

Report how many rooms are safe.
inf: First line: two integers N M
Next M lines: two integers a b (a one-way passage a->b)
outf: A single integer: the number of safe rooms
p12.exp: Room 3 has no outgoing passage -> safe. Rooms 1 and 2 form a cycle -> unsafe, and room 0 leads into that cycle -> unsafe. Exactly 1 safe room.

ans.pattern: Graph: reverse topological sort (peel off out-degree-0 nodes)
ans.brute: Cycle membership is subtle; peeling dead ends on the reversed graph marks exactly the safe nodes.
ans.opt: Repeatedly take nodes with current out-degree 0 (dead ends), mark them safe, and decrement the out-degree of their predecessors (via the reverse graph); newly-zero nodes join the queue. Count the safe nodes.

p13.title: Next Dip
p13.story:
A trail has N markers, each with a given elevation. For each marker, a hiker wants the elevation of the NEXT marker to the right that is strictly LOWER than the current one -- the first place, scanning rightward, where the trail drops below the current marker's height. If no later marker is lower, the answer for that marker is -1.

Produce this 'next lower to the right' value for every marker, in order. Equal elevations do not count as lower.

Report, for each marker in order, the next strictly lower elevation to its right, or -1.
inf: First line: integer N
Second line: N integers, the marker elevations
outf: A single line: N space-separated values, the next lower elevation or -1
p13.exp: Marker0 (4): next lower is 2. Marker1 (5): next lower is 2. Marker2 (2): none -> -1. Marker3 (10): next lower is 8. Marker4 (8): none -> -1. Output: 2 2 -1 8 -1.

ans.pattern: Monotonic stack (indices awaiting a lower neighbour)
ans.brute: Scanning right from each marker is O(N^2); a stack resolves each in amortised O(1).
ans.opt: Keep a stack of indices with non-decreasing elevation. For each new marker, pop every stacked index whose elevation is greater, setting its answer to the current elevation, then push the current index. Leftover indices get -1.

p14.title: Weakest Link Sum
p14.story:
A chain of N links each has an integer strength. For EVERY contiguous run of links, its 'weakest link' is the minimum strength in that run. The quality engineer wants the SUM, over all contiguous runs, of each run's weakest link.

There are about N*N/2 runs, so summing each run's minimum directly is too slow for large N. Because the answer can be large, report it modulo 1000000007.

Report the sum of the minimums of all contiguous runs, modulo 1000000007.
inf: First line: integer N
Second line: N integers, the link strengths
outf: A single integer: the sum of all subarray minimums modulo 1000000007
p14.exp: Summing the minimum of every contiguous run of [3,1,2,4] gives 17 (each element weighted by how many runs it is the minimum of).

ans.pattern: Monotonic stack (count runs where each element is the minimum)
ans.brute: Enumerating all runs is O(N^2); a monotonic stack finds, for each element, the span of runs in which it is the minimum.
ans.opt: For each element compute how many runs have it as the strict/tie-broken minimum, using a non-decreasing stack to find the distance to the previous smaller and next smaller-or-equal element; add value * leftCount * rightCount.

p15.title: Rung Gaps
p15.story:
A ladder maker has N rails, each cut to a distinct integer length, and wants to know how many PAIRS of rails differ in length by EXACTLY K units -- such pairs slot together into a standard fitting. The lengths are given unsorted and are all distinct.

Count the number of unordered pairs whose lengths differ by exactly K. Comparing every pair is too slow for large N; sorting first lets a two-pointer sweep count them in a single linear pass.

Report the number of pairs with length difference exactly K.
inf: First line: two integers N K
Second line: N integers, the distinct rail lengths
outf: A single integer: the number of pairs differing by exactly K
p15.exp: Sorted lengths 1,2,3,4,5. Pairs differing by exactly 2: (1,3), (2,4), (3,5) -> 3 pairs.

ans.pattern: Two pointers on the sorted lengths
ans.brute: Checking all O(N^2) pairs is too slow; a two-pointer sweep over sorted values counts them linearly.
ans.opt: Sort the lengths. Advance two pointers i and j: move i until a[i]-a[j] >= K; if it equals K (and i != j) count a pair; then advance j. Distinct values keep the count exact.
